reviewed.summary:
I read dashboard/src/engine.js end to end and checked it against app.js, template.html, countries.js, paper/index.qmd and model/ubi_model.py. The engine does what its code says. I found no code bug that changes a headline number:
- Re-running the default (200,000 histories, seed 20260929) reproduces every headline number in paper/results.json exactly: US 2.491% by 2040 and 7.431% by 2050, all ten 17.798%, US with no trigger 0.0053%, US endorsement by 2030 2.6235%, any of the ten 11.743%.
- The app's batch schedule (5,000, then 20,000 at a time) is bit-identical to one run for all ten countries.
- The vitest suite (82 tests) passes. The Python tests pass (7) once hypothesis is added, as CI does. Re-running the Python model reproduces model/results.json exactly.
- None of my 14 new fast-check properties failed, including 6x heavier re-runs. They covered pathwise monotonicity in the endorsement and passage multipliers, the lapse rule under alternating governments, country order and subset invariance, diffusion acting only after the first enactment, gridlock's scope, zero-hazard edges, every UI-reachable control setting (no NaN, no negative hazards, nothing above 1), batching at any split point, and endorsement-before-passage nesting.
- Large-sample sweeps found no risk switch, multiplier or trigger shift that moves any country's forecast the wrong way.

The blocker is a mismatch between what the page says and what the engine does. The ledger, the passage slider and the research prompt all state passage chances as "becomes law within the term" (US trifecta 55%, Westminster majorities 70%). The engine instead converts them to a yearly hazard over the full term length, starting the year after endorsement. In the simulation, endorsed UBIs become law within the term only about 15 to 35% of the time: US left-led 16.5% against a stated 55%, UK left-led 34.6% against 70%. The evidence cited for these inputs (Thomson et al. pledge fulfilment, US trifecta flagship priorities) measures within-term rates. So publishing as-is misstates a key falsifiable assumption. Fixing it changes the headline if the mechanism is changed to match the text; one illustrative variant gives US 4.7% and all ten 23.0% by 2040. Rewording the text instead leaves the headline alone but requires re-justifying the calibration.

The major finding: "shock under way" is never defined, and in the engine it is permanent from 1 to 3 years after the trigger through 2050. Several minors: Float32 onset masks, the "which is exact" claim, slider labels and caps, an impossible supposition that yields NaN, non-US triggers dated before October 2026, the PERT-accuracy comment, and wording on the ratchet and gridlock.

Scratch files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-review/engine/: props.mjs and props_heavy.mjs (the properties), within_term.mjs and within_term2.mjs (the blocker measurement), engine_instr.mjs, engine_v1.mjs and engine_shared.mjs (instrumented or variant copies of the engine), headline.mjs, and others.

I did not verify anything in a browser. Claude in Chrome was not connected, and the built-in browser cannot open file:// pages. The UI NaN finding is reproduced from app.js arithmetic, not from a rendered page.
checked: Headline reproduction: a fresh 200,000-history run (seed 20260929, default controls, scratchpad headline.mjs) matches paper/results.json exactly for US >=6.7% by 2040 (0.02491) and 2050 (0.07431), all ten by 2040 (0.17798), US given no trigger by 2040 (5.34e-5, shown as <0.1%), US endorsement by 2030 (0.026235), any of the ten endorsing by 2030 (0.11743) and US trigger by 2028 (0.08544).

Batching: the app's schedule (5,000, then 20,000 per batch, start offsets) equals one 200,000 run bit for bit for all ten countries: firstYear, firstEndorse, triggerYear, stateNext and onset (headline.mjs). Property P9 held for any split point and any controls (150 runs).

vitest: 82/82 pass (countries, differential, engine). Python: 7/7 pass with `uv run --with numpy --with pytest --with hypothesis python -m pytest -q` (the task's command omits hypothesis and fails at collection; CI and model/README use the correct one). Re-running ubi_model.simulate() without writing reproduces model/results.json exactly (py_check.py).

Per-term to per-year conversion: perYear(q,T) = 1-(1-clamp(q))^(1/T), with T = termYears (GBR/FRA 5, AUS 3, others 4). Endorsement and passage chances are clamped to [0,1] after multipliers, so no hazard can be negative or above 1 (P8 over the exact UI grid of shift, eL, eR, pass, amt, exposure and risks, 360 runs, checking hE, hEd, hP, ratchet, medians and amounts via the hook).

Endorsement lapse (engine.js:276): resets when the government type changes, and a new endorsement can happen that same year. P3a: yearly L/R (or L/O, R/O, L/R/O) alternation gives no UBI ever, even with endorse = pass = 1. P3b: two-year alternation gives endorsement in 2027 and law in 2028 in every history. Matches Python.
Endorsement strictly before passage within a year (the else-if at engine.js:285); per-history threshold years are nested (P11, any priors and controls, 240 runs).

Pathwise monotonicity: first enactment of any size never comes later when every endorsement multiplier is scaled up (P1), or when the passage multiplier is scaled up (P1b), for any priors and controls including diffusion (360 runs each). Distributional P2 and P2b (no-shock endorsement vs P(>=6.7%)) held. Crowd-out of big UBIs by early small ones did not appear even with tiny normal amounts and no ratchet (crowd.mjs).

Risk switches and multipliers against their descriptions (engine.js:137-140, 248-259, 266, 280, 286, 292): fiscal applies 0.6x per-term passage and 0.85x amounts including ratchet; meansTested 0.6x/0.8x per-term endorsement; diffusion 1.5x per-term endorsement from the year after any enactment (P5: nothing changes up to the first enactment year); gridlock 0.3x only in 'other' states (P6). With the real configs at 100,000 paired histories, no country/threshold/year cell moves the wrong way beyond 3 SE for any switch or 0.5x/2x multiplier (risk_mono.mjs).

Trigger shift slider: P(>=6.7%) and P(any size) by 2030/2040/2050 are monotone across shift -5..+10 for every country and for all ten at 50,000 histories (shift_sweep.mjs). The US onset clamp at 2026.75 holds.

Trigger bookkeeping: triggerYear = max(2026, floor(met)); shockFrom = ceil(met) + round(politics lag) matches Python's ceil(onset)+rint(lag). cumulativeOf counts 2026 in the 2027 bucket and equals a direct count for any subset and controls (P10).

Election and midterm handling: US periods reproduce the Python structure (2027 R 5% else divided; 2029 draw; midterm keep; later draws). The 0.98 cap never binds for the US (max sum 0.84), as the comment says. Using means per period instead of Python's shared per-history draws changes the US >=6.7% figure by at most 0.02 pp (paired SE 0.01-0.02 pp at 400,000 histories, engine_shared.mjs). JS 2.49% vs Python 2.53% by 2040.

Common random numbers: country streams are keyed on the ISO code. Permuting the ten countries changes nothing even with diffusion on (P4a); simulating any subset leaves each included country unchanged with diffusion off (P4b). With diffusion on, countries are coupled by design, which the paper's 'a change to one country's inputs leaves the others' results unchanged' does not mention. Stream-seed collisions: 502 of 2.2M (history, stream) seeds repeat, none within one history (seeds.mjs); negligible.

Zero-hazard edges: with every shock anchor at 0, onset is Infinity, triggerYear is never set, and shock-state endorsement priors change nothing (P7). Endorse 0 means no UBI, and pass 0 means endorsements but no UBI (existing tests).
Signpost conservation identity holds to 2.8e-17 for every signpost published in paper/results.json. Conditioning equals filtering (existing test).

PERT sampler: means within 9e-5 of the range of (lo+4m+hi)/6; central quantiles within 1e-4 of the range of exact beta.ppf (only the extreme tails are off; see finding). probit matches known values (existing test).
Scenario table default row (2.6% US) differs from the 2.5% headline because scenarios use 100,000 histories. The caption at paper/index.qmd:152 discloses this.
Build: bundling app.js, worker.js and template.html (same steps as build.js, output written to scratch) succeeds, 103 KB. Repo git status stayed clean throughout.

findings.claim: Ledger: 'If [a government type] has endorsed a UBI, it becomes law within the term' with value pertMean(pass), e.g. US left-led 55%, UK/Canada/Australia/France left-led 70%. The slider help (template.html:253) says 'Chance within the same term'. The engine comment (engine.js:130) says 'scales the chance an endorsed UBI becomes law within the term'. research/prompts/passage.md defines PASSAGE as 'becomes law within the same term' and asks for priors on 'passage given endorsement within a term'. passNote cites within-term fulfilment evidence (Thomson et al. 2017; US trifectas passed about half their flagship priorities).
findings.evidence: engine.js:253-256 converts q to a yearly hazard perYear(q, termYears) = 1-(1-q)^(1/termYears). engine.js:285 applies it only from the year after endorsement (the else-if bars passage in the endorsement year) and ignores how much of the term remains. So q is the chance of passing within termYears years after endorsement if the type holds, not within the term. Measured with an instrumented copy (scratchpad/.../engine/within_term2.mjs, 100,000 histories, default controls, endorsements whose term ends by 2050), realized P(law before the next general election | endorsed): USA L 0.165 (stated 0.55), USA R 0.155 (0.55), GBR L 0.346 (0.70), CAN L 0.309 (0.70), AUS L 0.301 (0.70), FRA L 0.346 (0.70), KOR L 0.343 (0.70), DEU L 0.226 (0.50), ESP L 0.206 (0.50), BRA L 0.118 (0.31). Conditioning on the type holding to term end still gives USA L 0.370 and GBR L 0.346. A related point, computed from the formula: the US endorsement row says 'within its 4-year term' (60% in a shock), but a US trifecta usually lasts 2 years, and 1-(1-0.6)^(2/4) = 0.37. The same wording is in model/ubi_model.py:106, so the differential test cannot catch it. Decision impact, from an illustrative variant (engine_v1.mjs) that spreads the stated q over the years left in the period: US >=6.7% by 2040 is 4.66% (current 2.49%), by 2050 13.02% (7.43%); all ten by 2040 23.00% (17.80%). The paper's own scenario 'Endorsed UBIs pass twice as often' gives 7.0% for the US and 30% for all ten.
findings.fix: Choose one. (a) Keep the mechanism and reword the ledger, slider help, engine comment, Python comment and paper so the input reads as 'chance it becomes law within N years of endorsement while the same type of government holds power (yearly X%)'. Then re-justify the numbers, since the cited evidence measures within-term rates. (b) Keep the wording and change the hazard so the stated q is the realized within-term (or within-spell) chance, e.g. spread q over the years remaining in the period. Add a test that measures the realized within-term passage rate against the ledger value. Re-run results.mjs and republish the numbers.
findings.decision_impact: Blocks publishing as-is: the ledger presents as falsifiable an input the engine does not implement, and it is roughly double what the model delivers. Rewording clears this without moving the headline. Honoring the stated within-term rates raises the US 2040 figure from about 2.5% to roughly 4 to 5%, and all ten from 17.8% to about 23% (one variant), so the owner must decide which it is before publishing revision 2.

findings.claim: The ledger conditions six endorsement inputs per country on 'while the shock is under way' / 'with no shock under way' (app.js:353), resolved 'Only if that government holds power under that condition'. The paper says endorsement depends on 'whether the trigger's shock is under way' (index.qmd:86).
findings.evidence: engine.js:238 sets x.shockFrom = ceil(met) + polLag once per history. engine.js:274 uses shock = y >= x.shockFrom. No code path ends a shock. Once under way it lasts through 2050, even if 12-month unemployment later falls back below the trigger level. It also counts as 'no shock' for the 0-2 year politics lag after the trigger is met. Neither the ledger, the paper nor the template defines when a shock is under way or ends.
findings.fix: Define the condition observably in the ledger and paper, e.g. 'from 1 to 3 calendar years after the trigger year through 2050, whatever unemployment does afterwards'. Alternatively, model shock end if that is intended.
findings.decision_impact: Does not change the headline. It leaves half of each country's conditional endorsement inputs unresolvable as written, which undercuts the 'everything falsifiable' goal. Fix before publishing.

findings.claim: Signpost masks 'The US trigger is met by the end of 2030/2035' and 'has not been met by 2040' (app.js:120-122; results.mjs) use sim.onset. Everything else (shockFrom, triggerYear, Checkable soon) uses the double-precision date.
findings.evidence: onset is stored in a Float32Array (engine.js:198, 227). scratchpad f32.mjs at 200,000 histories, seed 20260929, found 5 histories where float32 rounding pushes the onset up to an integer year, so the mask disagrees with triggerYear. Examples: history 121097 has triggerYear 2040 but float32 onset 2041 (counted as 'not met by 2040'), and history 32345 has 2035 vs 2036. No effect on UBI-by-2040 events, because shockFrom already starts at 2041 or later in those cases.
findings.fix: Store onset as Float64Array, or build the trigger signpost masks from triggerYear.
findings.decision_impact: Negligible (5 of 200,000 histories). A consistency fix only.

findings.claim: 'Election, midterm and exposure inputs each feed a single yes-or-no draw per history, so the engine uses their means, which is exact.' engine.js:155-158 says the same ('same distribution').
findings.evidence: engine.js:163-165 applies the 0.98 left+right cap to the means. Drawing pL and pR per history and capping each draw gives different election odds wherever hi(pL)+hi(pR) > 0.98 (scratchpad capmean.mjs, 400,000 draws). ESP 2028 'other' is 3.8% in the engine vs 5.9% with per-draw capping, ESP 2032+ 5.0% vs 7.0%, BRA 2027 2.0% vs 4.1%, JPN 2030 7.0% vs 7.1%. Headline effect (capmean_effect.mjs, 200,000 histories): all ten by 2040 is 17.798% vs 17.765%, ESP 2.142% vs 2.087%, US unchanged. Also, election draws are three-way, not yes-or-no.
findings.fix: Say 'exact except where a range's left+right can exceed 0.98; there the cap is applied to the means', or cap per draw.
findings.decision_impact: Wording only; headline effect 0.03 pp.

findings.claim: The endorsement slider help says 'Chance within a term during a shock'. The amount slider is labeled 'Amount if enacted during a shock'. The endorsement slider readout caps at 98%.
findings.evidence: engine.js:247 multiplies every endorsement input, no-shock ones included, by ctl.endorse. engine.js:258-259 multiplies both amount.normal and amount.shock (and so ratchet redraws) by ctl.amount. app.js:407-408 caps the displayed value with Math.min(0.98, ...). The engine clamps each draw at 1 (perYear, engine.js:122), so at eL=+2 the display shows 98% while every US left-led government in a shock has a per-term chance of 1. The ledger always shows unscaled priors while its help says the sliders scale 'every country's explicit value'.
findings.fix: Say the endorsement slider scales no-shock chances too, and the amount slider scales no-shock amounts too. Use min(1, ...) in the readout, or show the capped mean over draws.
findings.decision_impact: Polish; no effect on default numbers.

findings.claim: No control should produce NaN.
findings.evidence: A reachable sequence: click 'Suppose this' on 'The US trigger is met by the end of 2030', then move 'When the US trigger is met' to +5 years or more. A shared link #shift=5&if=ai2030 does the same. update() keeps the supposition because the id still exists in signpostDefs(). With shift +5 every onset is at or after 2031.75, so the mask is empty. Reproducing app.js's arithmetic in scratchpad nan_ui.mjs gives: 0 matching histories, cumulative p = NaN, yMax = Math.max(...NaN, 0.02) = NaN, niceMax(NaN) = 1, and SVG path y = NaN. The hero shows '–', the curve's y-axis jumps to 100% with an invisible series, and the active signpost row disappears (it is filtered by 0<pS<1). Not observed in a rendered browser: Chrome extension not connected, and the built-in pane cannot open file://.
findings.fix: Clear state.cond (or show 'no histories match') when the condition mask is empty. Guard lineChart's yMax against NaN.
findings.decision_impact: UX only; no wrong number displayed.

findings.claim: 'The trigger has not been met as of October 2026' (engine.js:226). The clamp is applied to the US onset only.
findings.evidence: met = on + lag with negative lags (GBR, CAN, AUS lo -0.5; KOR lo -1) is not clamped. scratchpad early_met.mjs (200,000 histories) finds triggers dated before 2026.75 in 456 histories at default (KOR 281, CAN 109, AUS 37, GBR 29) and 11,803 at shift -5. Because of ceil(), this only matters when met <= 2026.0, which happened for KOR in 1 history at default and 237 (0.12%) at shift -5; there the shock regime starts a year early. triggerYear is clamped to 2026 and counted in the first year, so the 'Checkable soon' trigger figures are unaffected.
findings.fix: Clamp met to at least 2026.75 for every country.
findings.decision_impact: Negligible at default.

findings.claim: The PERT inverse-CDF table is 'accurate to well under 0.1% of the range'.
findings.evidence: scratchpad pert_q.mjs compared the table's quantiles with scipy beta.ppf. Error is under 1e-4 of the range for u in [0.001, 0.999] and means are within 9e-5 of the range (pert_mean.mjs). In the outer 1/1024 tails, linear interpolation to q[0]=0 or q[M]=1 errs by up to 1.3% of the range (US L_shock at u=0.9995) and 9% (mode-at-lo shapes, JPN amount 4.6%).
findings.fix: Qualify the comment ('except the outer 0.1% tails') or add finer tail nodes.
findings.decision_impact: Code comment only; no measurable effect on outputs.

findings.claim: 'During a shock, a governing majority can raise an existing program in any year.' The gridlock switch (engine.js:140) acts 'under divided government, cross-bloc coalitions and hung parliaments'.
findings.evidence: engine.js:291 allows the ratchet only when st !== 0, so 'other' governments never raise a program. For Germany and Spain, 'other' includes majority grand coalitions (countries.js electionNote). engine.js:255 applies gridlock to every 'other' state, and for Brazil 'other' is 'a centrist president' (countries.js:278), which is not divided or coalition government as described.
findings.fix: Say 'a left- or right-led government' for the ratchet, and list each country's 'other' in the gridlock text (or exempt BRA).
findings.decision_impact: Wording; no default-number effect.

findings.claim: 'the tests check it for every signpost', and index.qmd:172 says 'every signpost averages back to today's forecast'.
findings.evidence: dashboard/test/engine.test.js:35-38 checks conservation for one signpost only (US onset < 2031). The identity does hold for all published signposts: max |pS*pIfYes+(1-pS)*pIfNo-pU| over every signpost in paper/results.json is 2.8e-17, which I computed this session.
findings.fix: Either loop the test over all signpostDefs, or say the identity holds by construction and is tested on one signpost.
findings.decision_impact: Wording or test coverage only.

reviewed.summary:
I found no semantic drift between the Python reference and the JS engine for the US. The two agree at 20M histories each: US $6k by 2040 is 2.519% (JS) vs 2.518% (Python), and all 20 compared statistics are within |z|<2, including endorsement by 2030 and the no-trigger conditional. model/inputs.json equals countries.js exactly, and results.json reproduces bit-for-bit.

The only structural difference is how election priors are shared. Python reuses one draw across the five later elections and five midterms; JS draws each period independently. The effect is negligible (≤0.006 pp).

Two major issues should be settled before publishing:
1. **Stale model README.** model/README.md (public repo, not updated in revision 2) still shows revision-1 results (9.6% by 2040, 23% by 2050, a nonexistent q_any input, revision-1 structure). The paper points readers to this Python reference.
2. **Midterm lapse rule (shared by both implementations).** An endorsement lapses when the government type changes, so a US President's endorsement lapses at a midterm flip even though the head of government, who per the paper's own definition made it, stays. The ledger's '60% within its 4-year term' also cannot resolve for a trifecta the model usually ends after 2 years (implied tenure probability 43%). With no lapse at midterms, the US figure moves from 2.5% to 3.0% by 2040 and from 7.4% to 9.4% by 2050. This is a stated modeling choice, not a code bug, so it is the owner's call.

Minor issues:
- The differential test's 5-SE tolerance, anchored at a seed-11 run that sits z≈-2 below Python, would pass a +0.24 pp US 2040 drift. Five of 12 plausible single-line engine bugs pass the whole test.
- There is no deterministic check that the JS and Python inputs match, that results.json is fresh, or that endorsement agrees.
- export_radiant.py crashes (KeyError q_any_D_normal), and its map files carry revision-1 numbers.
- The Python docstring and shock notes still describe the revision-1 yearly hazard and an 'economist-attributed' shock, not the measurable trigger.

All scratch scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-review/python-parity/.
checked: Python tests: 7 passed with `uv run --with pytest --with numpy --with hypothesis pytest -q`, run in a scratch copy of model/. The task's command without hypothesis fails at import; CI (test.yml) and both READMEs include hypothesis, so this is not a repo defect.
JS: dashboard/test/differential.test.js 6/6 pass; full `bunx vitest run` 82/82 pass (countries 62, differential 6, engine 14). The repo was left unchanged (git status clean, HEAD 2b027ba).
model/results.json reproduces bit-for-bit from the current ubi_model.simulate() (numpy 2.5.3; cumulative, m2 and attribution identical).

model/inputs.json equals the current INPUTS. All 24 US-relevant values equal countries.js: GLOBALS shock_by_* and politics_lag; periods 2027/2029/later/keep; endorse L/R/O normal/shock = e_D/e_R/e_div; pass L/R/O; amount normal/shock via usd(); ratchet. US termYears defaults to 4, exposure R(1,1,1), lag R(0,0,0), signpostPeriod 1 = 2029.

Line-by-line semantics match between ubi_model.py and engine.js:
- Onset CDF: anchors [2026.75, 2029, 2031, 2036, 2041, 2051], monotone forcing, piecewise-linear.
- shock_from = ceil(onset) + round(lag). rint and Math.round differ only at exact .5, which has probability zero.
- Government coding: 0/1/2 = O/L/R. 2027 is an R-only draw; 2029 is a three-way draw on one uniform.
- Election calendar: midterm keep in 2031, 2035, ..., 2047; presidential draws in 2033, ..., 2049.
- The D+R caps never bind (max sum 0.84 < 0.9 < 0.98).
- Each year: lapse first, then endorse or pass (never both in one year).
- Passage uses the current government type.
- Amount: lognormal, sigma 0.6 normal / 0.5 shock, floored at $1,000 (JS 1.11%).
- Ratchet: a yearly probability with no term conversion, only in a shock under a non-divided government (including the enactment year), redraw sigma 0.5, taking the max.
- Thresholds are recorded after the ratchet.
- Years simulated: 2027-2050.
Controls: DEFAULT_CONTROLS (risks all off, multipliers 1, exposure 'model', shift 0) equals the dashboard's DEFAULT_STATE through controlsFrom().
Threshold conversions: 6.665% x $90,027 = $6,000.30 and 1.11% = $999.30, against Python's $6,000 and $1,000. The difference is negligible.

20M-history differential (JS seed 12345 vs Python seeds 1000-1019, n_scen=1): all 20 statistics agree within |z|<2.
- $6k by 2040: 2.5194% vs 2.5184%.
- $6k by 2050: 7.4150% vs 7.4213%.
- $1k by 2036: 1.6227% vs 1.6240%.
- Endorsement by 2030: 2.5646% vs 2.5594%.
- P(UBI by 2040 | no trigger by 2040): 1.17e-4 vs 1.15e-4, which supports the '<0.1%' claim.
- P(UBI by 2040 | D trifecta 2029): 2.73% vs 2.74%.
- P(UBI by 2040 | trigger by 2030): 9.45% in both.

Paper headline US numbers reproduce exactly with the paper's seed and n (200k, seed 20260929): 2040 = 2.491%, 2050 = 7.431%, endorsement by 2030 = 2.6235%. US results are identical whether the US runs alone or with all ten countries. Four batches of 10k with start offsets equal one 40k run (all ten countries).

The JS PERT inverse-CDF table is accurate: across 135 ranges, max quantile error is 3.4e-6 of the range and max mean error 4.3e-5 of the range (checked against scipy beta.ppf). This supports the 'well under 0.1%' claim.
Python's 200k x 5 clustering does not materially distort the test's SE formula: the design effect over 30 seeds is about 1 (0.65-1.42, noisy).
Mutation testing: the differential test does catch no lapse, same-year endorse+pass, termYears 2, lag floor, shock floor, and divided passage using the left-led prior.

Paper l.170 (five SE at 2032, 2036, 2040, 2045, 2050; the Python run of 1,000,000 gives 2.5%, actual 2.532%) is accurate. Paper l.90 ('Shock-driven endorsements begin one to three years after a country's trigger is met') matches the code: ceil(met) + round(PERT(0,1,2)). app.js l.377 ('The Python model's tests check the same for year and amount') matches test_ubi_model.py.

findings.claim: An endorsement lapses whenever the government type changes, and US endorsement chances are stated per 4-year term. Paper line 86 says: 'An endorsement means a statement by the head of government, or a governing party's platform ... It lapses when the type of government changes.' The ledger (app.js ~l.351) says a US left-led government 'endorses a qualifying UBI within its 4-year term' at 60% during a shock.
findings.evidence: Both implementations apply this rule: ubi_model.py l.211 `endorsed = np.where((endorsed >= 0) & (endorsed != c), -1, endorsed)` and engine.js l.276. So the rule is not a parity issue. For the US, the government type is set per Congress, so a Democratic-trifecta President's endorsement lapses when the House or Senate flips at a midterm, even though the head of government who made it is still in office. Python's own input then asks 'The President endorses under divided government' again (e_div_shock). I made a scratch variant of engine.js with no lapse in midterm ('keep') periods (scratch mut/engine_V1_no_lapse_at_midterm.js, n=4,000,000, seed 99). US $6k by 2040 went from 2.506% to 3.049%, and by 2050 from 7.414% to 9.360%. The 4-year-term wording has a second problem. With the midterm-survival prior (mean 0.258), a US trifecta usually lasts 2 years. The chance that a D trifecta endorses while it holds power during a shock is then 0.742 x 0.372 + 0.258 x 0.600 = 43.1% (computed from PERT(0.35,0.6,0.85)), not the 60% the ledger shows. When the trifecta ends at the midterm, the 60% proposition cannot resolve.
findings.fix: For the US (and other presidential systems), tie endorsement to the head of government. Lapse only when the presidency changes hands or party, not at midterms. Or state and justify the midterm lapse explicitly. Phrase the ledger proposition over the government's actual tenure, or show the tenure-implied probability. Apply the same change to ubi_model.py so parity holds.
findings.decision_impact: This is not a code bug: the code does what the paper says. But the stated rule conflicts with the paper's own definition of endorsement for the US. Under the no-midterm-lapse reading, the US headline moves from 2.5% to 3.0% by 2040 and from 7.4% to 9.4% by 2050. The owner should decide before publishing whether to keep the rule, with a justification, or change it and re-run.

findings.claim: The model README presents the Python reference's current result as 9.6% by 2040 and 23.0% by 2050, with revision-1 signposts, sensitivities and attribution.

reviewed.summary: The published numbers are reproducible: re-running the current engine matches every headline in _variables.yml, and revision 1's 9.6% reproduces from origin/main. The risk toggles, lapse rule, exposure modes and signpost logic match the code, and no copy implies an interval around a probability. Two mechanism claims are materially wrong, though. (1) The trigger does not do what the copy says. The eleven-episode test only checked GDP in the first month of each rise. Applying the trigger as actually defined (12-month unemployment at least 3 points above a baseline-year average while GDP is at or above its previous peak) to the repo's own FRED data, it is met in the recovery after every large US recession (1975, 1983, 2010, 2021) and in recoveries in eight other countries. So 'separates a technology shock from an ordinary recession', 'without a recession' and 'if no AI shock' are false. The trigger's probabilities are also revision 1's AI-shock priors, carried over unchanged. (2) The ledger presents per-term hazard parameters as observable propositions. The model itself implies that an endorsed US trifecta UBI passes before the trifecta ends about 17% of the time (27% even over a full term), against the stated 55%, and that a shock-era Democratic trifecta endorses 43% of the time, against 60%. The UK passage figure is about 34% against 70%. Major issues: the Revisions text misattributes the drop from 9.6% to 2.5%. The lapse rule accounts for about 3 to 4.5 points and new, lower shock-stage judgments (not mentioned) for about 1.5 to 3; the no-shock 'record' accounts for about 0.1. The generosity multiplier and amounts are unchanged, not replaced. The 'no endorsement in 75 terms' record is contradicted by the repo's own facts (Brazil's 2004 law; Korea's governing-party pledge in 2022). Other countries can meet their trigger only if the US does, which is unstated and contradicted by history. The ledger amount rows describe the median prior rather than the amount drawn: 26 to 34% of draws fall outside the stated ranges, and the dispersion, floor and shock permanence have no ledger row. The paper's 'dividend-scale' description is false for 6 of 10 countries. The wrapper implies $6,000 for all ten countries. The meta tags claim 'every assumption adjustable and every input sourced'. Recommendation: do not publish revision 2 as-is. The trigger and ledger fixes are copy changes if the model is kept, but the trigger definition probably needs rethinking because it is the event everything is conditioned on.

The model's trigger is a different test: a level at least 3 points above a fixed baseline-year average, held while real GDP is at or above its previous peak. Scratch script wf-review/claims/backtest_trigger_strict.py applies the trigger as defined to the repo's own FRED CSVs, using completed GDP quarters only. With the pre-recession year as the baseline, the US trigger is met in the recovery after every large recession: 1975-12 (1973 baseline, 12-month average 8.47 against a 7.86 level, 1975Q4 GDP 6184.5 above the prior peak 6150.1), 1983-06 (1979 baseline), 2010-12 (2007 baseline, 12-month average 9.61 against 7.62, 2010Q4 GDP 16960.9 above 16943.3) and 2021-03 (2019 baseline, 8.70 against 6.68, 2021Q1 GDP 21106.6 above 20985.4). votes.reasoning:
The finding holds. The copy says the GDP condition "separates a labor-displacing technology shock from an ordinary recession" (app.js:373, index.qmd:74). It also says the forecast depends on "a labor shock of a kind the United States has not seen" (index.qmd:38) and that unemployment rises "without a recession" (index.qmd:8). All of these are false for the trigger as the copy defines it.

1. The "eleven episodes" figure is correct, but only for a different test. I re-ran compute_triggers.py on a scratch copy and the output matches triggers.json exactly. That script checks for a 3-point rise over 24 months and looks at GDP only in the first month of each episode.

2. The published trigger is a different test. It needs the 12-month average at or above the 2025 average plus 3 (7.3% for the US) while real GDP is at or above its previous peak. I applied that test to the repo's own FRED data, using completed GDP quarters only. The US meets it in the recovery after almost every large recession: 1975-12, 1981-03, 1983-06, 1992-07, 2010-12 and 2021-03. For example, in 2010-12 the 12-month average was 9.61 against a 7.62 threshold, and 2010Q4 GDP was 16960.9 against a prior peak of 16943.3.

3. A stricter reading does not rescue the claim. If the trigger counts only in the month the 12-month average first crosses 7.3%, it still fires in July 1992. The average went from 7.23 to 7.31, and 1992Q2 GDP was 10347.4, above its prior peak of 10236.4. That was the jobless recovery after the 1990–91 recession, not a technology shock.

4. Other countries show the same recovery-period hits, measured from a pre-recession baseline year: GBR 1993-09, FRA 1994-03, DEU 2005-07, ESP 2016-12, JPN 2003-06, KOR 1999-06, CAN 1983-12 and 1993-06, AUS 1983-12 and 1992-06.

5. The trigger probabilities price only an AI shock. GLOBALS shock_by_* is byte-identical to revision 1 on origin/main, and the notes cite AGI and AI-unemployment markets. engine.js:214 draws the US onset only from those numbers; there is no recession path.

6. Ordinary business cycles alone would have met the trigger about as often as the model expects an AI shock to. Take each year as a baseline, set the threshold at that year's average plus 3, and ask whether the trigger is met in the following years. The US did so within 3 years in 8% of years (6/75), within 5 years in 19% (14/73) and within 15 years in 52% (33/63). The model's priors are 8% by 2028, 18% by 2030 and 43% by 2040. So the "Checkable soon" trigger predictions (US 8.5% by 2028, 18.4% by 2030, confirmed in paper/results.json) could resolve YES from an ordinary recession followed by a slow recovery. They would not test the AI-shock assumption the copy says they test. That undercuts the owner's stated goal that every assumption be falsifiable.

7. Brazil's history was never checked (triggers.json u_start 2024-09; the countries.js note says "History not checked"). The claim "In the official records of all ten countries" (index.qmd:74) is therefore overstated. This part is minor.

8. One part of the finding is overstated. The table caption at index.qmd:124 does say the last column "conditions on the US trigger not being met by 2040". So the "if no AI shock" column header is a minor label mismatch, not a separate false claim.

The headline numbers do not change as published. The severity is still blocker: under the task's definition, the page and paper state something false about the event that "nearly all of that probability runs through".

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and I rate it a blocker.

**The copy states the claim.** app.js:373 (the "How it works" section) says "the second condition separates a labor-displacing technology shock from an ordinary recession." index.qmd:74 says the same. The paper also describes the trigger as a rise:
- "without a recession" (abstract, :8)
- "while the economy keeps growing" (:34)
- "a labor shock of a kind the United States has not seen" (:38)
- "leaves output growing and employment falling" (:182)

The model figure in build_assets.py:241 labels the trigger "unemployment +3 points without a recession". The table column is "By 2040 if no AI shock" (build_assets.py:119, table_countries.md). The same text appears in the built dashboard/dist/index.html and paper/index.html.

**The eleven-episode test checks something different from the trigger.** compute_triggers.py checks GDP only in the first month that the 12-month average rises 3 points above its value 24 months earlier. So "in all eleven, GDP was below its previous peak" is true for that test. It does not follow that the trigger as defined excludes recessions. The trigger is a 12-month average at or above a fixed baseline-year level plus 3, held while GDP is at or above its previous peak. The 12-month average lags, and GDP recovers first, so the trigger fires during recoveries.

**My own backtest with today's exact US level shows this.** I applied the 7.3% level to the repo's UNRATE and GDPC1 files, using completed quarters only. The trigger would have been met in 1975-12, 1981-03, 1983-06, 1992-07, 2010-12 and 2021-03. That is the recovery from every major US recession since 1975, including 1990-91. The reviewer's GDP figures match the CSV: 2010Q4 16960.864 against the 2008Q2 peak of 16943.291, and 2021Q1 21106.619 against 2019Q4 20985.448. I also ran the test over every baseline year for all nine FRED countries. Recovery hits appear in GBR 1993, FRA 1994, DEU 2005, ESP 2016, JPN 2003, KOR 1999, and AUS 1983 and 1992. Canada is also hit in 1978 after only a two-quarter dip in 1974-75.

**Ordinary recessions alone roughly match the model's AI prior.** Starting two years after each US baseline year, the trigger as defined was met:

| Horizon | Recessions alone, history | Model (AI-anchored) |
|---|---|---|
| Within 3 years | 8% | 8.5% by 2028 |
| Within 5 years | 19% | 18.4% by 2030 |
| Within 15 years | 52% | 44% by 2040 |
| Within 25 years | 75% | prior mode 0.55 by 2050 |

The historical windows overlap and rest on about six recessions, so these are rough. Even so, the published "Checkable soon" US trigger predictions (8.5% by 2028, 18.4% by 2030) equal the base rate from ordinary recessions. A YES would say nothing about the AI assumption. That undercuts the owner's goal of making assumptions falsifiable.

**The trigger probabilities are still revision 1's AI priors.** I confirmed with `git show origin/main` that GLOBALS `shock_by_*` are the same as revision 1's, and the notes still cite AGI and AI-unemployment markets.

**Recession-driven triggers would get AI-shock endorsement rates.** Once a trigger fires, the model applies the shock-state endorsement rates (US L_shock mode 0.6 per term, O_shock 0.4). The 2010 and 2021 recovery hits were followed by no UBI endorsement under Obama or Biden. That is only two cases, but it does not fit those rates.

**Brazil's history was not checked.** triggers.json has BRA u_start 2024-09, and the ledger says "History not checked", so "across the ten countries" and "the official records of all ten countries" overstate the test. I did not verify Brazil's 2015-17 history myself.

**Impact on the numbers.** The engine never evaluates the trigger definition: engine.js:214-226 draws onset from the PERT priors. So the copy does not change a headline number mechanically. But the definition is how published predictions resolve. As shipped, a careful reader, and anyone resolving the Checkable soon predictions, would believe the trigger isolates a technology shock, when it fires after ordinary recessions at about the rate the model gives. That is a false statement about the model's central event, in the abstract, the figure, the table header and the dashboard. Under the rubric that is a blocker.

**The fix that keeps the numbers is to redefine the trigger.** That changes the resolution criteria but can leave the headline. Keeping the definition would instead mean re-pricing the priors and the shock-state endorsement rates. The headline would then change, and I cannot say in which direction without a run.

- Another option: require the unemployment rise itself to occur while GDP is at new peaks.

- AUS left-led (ledger 70%): 32.0%.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and it goes deeper than a labeling problem.

Mechanics, read directly in dashboard/src/engine.js:
- Line 122 (`perYear`) turns each per-term value into a constant yearly hazard over `termYears`. For the US that is 4.
- Line 276 cancels an endorsement when the government type changes.
- The `else if` at line 285 means a UBI can pass at the earliest the year after it is endorsed.
- US periods are 2 years long. The midterm `keep` prior averages about 25% (countries.js:32).

What the ledger says, in app.js:353 and 357: "If [a left-led government] has endorsed a UBI, it becomes law within the term: 55%" and "...endorses a qualifying UBI within its 4-year term: 60%". The "Resolves" column describes these as observable events.

What the engine actually implies, from my own instrumented copy (100k histories, all ten countries):
- **US passage:** 18.5% of Democratic-trifecta endorsements become law before the trifecta ends, against 55% in the ledger. For Republican trifectas it is 18.1% (ledger 55%). For divided government it is 6.0% (ledger 10.5%).
- **US endorsement during a shock:** a Democratic trifecta endorses before it leaves power 42.1% of the time (ledger 60%). For Republican trifectas it is 23.9% (ledger 35.8%). 75% of observed US trifecta spells are shorter than 4 years.
- **Passage elsewhere:** the model's rate is below the ledger in every country. It is 1.4 to 2.9 times lower for left-led governments (UK 42.9% vs 70%, Canada 41.9% vs 70%, Japan 24.6% vs 50%). The current UK Labour government is 39.7% vs 70%.
- **Endorsement outside the US:** roughly matches the ledger, because those terms are fixed-length.
- **Where the ledger is exact:** I measured passage within exactly `term` years after the endorsement year, with the same government holding power throughout. That gave US 53.9%, UK 70.0% and Korea 69.3%. Endorsement under full-term shock exposure gave US 58.9% and UK 45.3%. So the ledger values are exact only in the hypothetical where the government holds power for a full term, counted from the year after it endorses. The reviewer's description holds. My numbers differ from theirs by a few points because I defined spells differently (for example 18.5% vs 16.5%, and UK 39.7% vs 33.9%). The direction and size agree.

Why I rate this a blocker and not major:

1. **It breaks revision 2's stated purpose.** The goal is "everything falsifiable incl assumptions". The dashboard says "Every assumption is stated so it can turn out wrong... The ledger gives each assumption's resolution" (app.js:375). The paper says "Every input is a proposition that can turn out false" and "scores will be added as they resolve" (index.qmd:158, 166). Scoring the ledger rows would test numbers the model does not use: 55% where the model commits to about 18%. The slider readout shows the same 55% labeled "Chance within the same term" (template.html:253).

2. **It hides a mismatch between the input and its cited data.** The US passage prior is tagged "DATA: about half of US trifectas' flagship priorities since 1993 passed" (model/ubi_model.py:107; passNote in countries.js). That record is a rate per trifecta, and most of those trifectas lasted 2 years. The model applies it as a 4-year hazard to trifectas that mostly last 2 years and endorse mid-spell, so its actual rate is about 18%. If passage is scaled so the model's per-trifecta rate is about 58% (pass ×2), US $6k by 2040 goes from 2.55% to 7.03%, and at least one of the ten goes from 17.8% to 29.6%. Readers are told passage is anchored to data at 55%. The model's operative value is about a third of that, and the gap alone moves the US headline by nearly 3 times.

3. **Only one part of the copy is protected.** The paper's methods section discloses the per-term to yearly conversion (index.qmd:86 and the tbl-inputs caption at 112). That protects a careful paper reader there. The dashboard ledger, the slider copy and the paper's falsification section (index.qmd:166) all present the full-term value as the observable probability.

The headline does not change as published. My copy with only a trace hook reproduces 2.55% (US) and 17.8% (any of ten). The bug is not in the engine. What is false is what the ledger says the engine assumes, and the numbers are off by up to 3 times.

What the defect does not touch: "Checkable soon", the signposts and the market comparisons are all computed from the simulation (app.js renderSoon uses `cumulativeOf` on sim arrays), so those tests are correct.

**What reproduced.** I ran my own decomposition from primary sources:

**Drivers of the 7.1-point drop.** The split depends on the order of the steps, so I ran two paths. The ranges below span both.
- Lapse rule: about 3.1 to 4.8 points, the largest driver.
  - Path 1: 8.92% to 4.17%.
  - Path 2: 5.62% to 2.49%.
- Passage coming at least a year after endorsement ("takes time"): about 1.1 to 1.2 points.
  - 10.13% to 8.92%, and 6.76% to 5.62%.
- Lower shock-state judgments, which the copy never mentions: about 1.6 to 2.9 points.
  - Per-term endorse x pass means are L 33.0%, R 19.7%, O 4.3%, against revision 1's q of 45.8%, 25.8% and 8.3%.
  - With the lapse: 4.17% to 2.60%.
  - In the revision 1 engine: 9.54% to 6.74%.
- No-shock recalibration: about 0.08 to 0.11 points.
  - Revision 1 engine: 9.62% to 9.54%.
  - Revision 2 engine: 2.60% to 2.49%.
  - It is small because a no-shock UBI starts near $2,000 and rarely reaches the $6,000 bar.

- app.js:379 gives three reasons for the drop. One of them, "the record rules out the no-shock rates revision 1 implied", accounts for about 1.5% of the drop.
- A driver worth about 22 to 40% of the drop (lower shock-state endorse x pass) is left out.
- The paper's "Both changes lower the forecast" (index.qmd:186) is technically true, but it implies the recalibration matters for the headline, and it does not.
- This is a wrong causal explanation of a published change. It does not alter any number, so it is major, not a blocker.

**Where the finding overstates (sub-point 4).** The finding says nothing replaced "generosity" with explicit amounts. In the engine, revision 2's amount slider is indeed the same multiplier as revision 1's generosity (revision 1 engine.js:240-241, revision 2 :258-259). But the UI did change what the controls show:
- Revision 1 showed "Political appetite x1.5" and "Generosity x1.5" (origin/main app.js:365-366).
- Revision 2 shows explicit US values: endorsement %, passage %, and a dollar "Amount if enacted during a shock" (app.js:407-411, template.html:240-260).

- **Lower shock-state judgments: large and unmentioned.** Revision 2's per-term endorse-times-pass products during a shock are lower than revision 1's q: L 0.33 vs 0.458, R 0.197 vs 0.258, O 0.043 vs 0.083. That costs 1.4 to 2.75 points: 9.62% to 6.87% in revision 1's engine, 4.08% to 2.65% with lapse, 8.21% to 5.60% without.
- **Lapse: the biggest single driver.** Turning it off moves 2.49% to 5.62%. At revision 1-matched products it moves 8.21% to 4.08%.
- **Two-step timing: about 1.4 points.** Revision 1's 9.62% falls to 8.21% under revision 2's structure with no lapse and per-term products matched to revision 1.

One ordered chain: 9.62 → 8.21 (two steps) → 4.08 (lapse) → 2.65 (shock judgments) → 2.52 (no-shock recalibration). A control run with pass rescaled gives 2.52% against the actual 2.49%. The split into parts depends on the order and on how each product is divided between endorsement and passage, but the ranking holds in every combination I ran.

"Rules out" is too strong. The dashboard's own ledger note says a 3% per-term rate leaves an 11% chance of the clean record (0.97^75 = 0.102). Revision 1's US L_normal of 3.33% leaves 7.9%. Revision 1's no-shock q averaged across countries and government types was about 1.2% per term, which leaves about 40%. So the record is consistent with revision 1's no-shock rates.

The finding's point 4 (generosity) is only partly right. Amount, ratchet, exposure, lag, periods, termYears and GLOBALS are identical in both revisions for all 10 countries, and the amount slider is still a plain multiplier. But revision 2 did replace the "Political appetite ×" and "Generosity ×" sliders with sliders that show explicit US values (a percent, or dollars from US.amount.shock), so the phrase is defensible as a description of the controls. It is not offered as a cause of the drop, so at most it is minor wording.

Why major and not blocker: no headline number changes, and each named mechanism does push the forecast down. Why major and not minor: both the Revisions section and the paper tell readers why the forecast fell, and a careful reader would come away wrong. They would think the calibration to the record mattered and that the during-shock judgments were unchanged. That is a false statement about how the model works, which the owner's rules and his falsifiability goal both target. It also matters because his own Manifold markets opened at revision 1's odds. The staged maxghenis.com PR #62 carries both passages verbatim, so this ships if published as-is.

Confirmed:

Art. 1 creates a renda básica de cidadania as the right of all residents "não importando sua condição socioeconômica", paid annually. §2 sets an equal amount for everyone, enough for minimum food, education and health costs. The only escape is §1: coverage comes in stages at the executive's discretion, poorest first.

So a right-led government also wrote UBI universalization into statute.

(5) The "data" label is shown to readers. (b) 11% vs 10%. 0.97^75 = 10.18% (binomial), but exp(-0.03*75) = 10.54% (Poisson), which rounds to 11%. Both 47% figures are consistent (47.06%, 47.24%). "About 11%" is a defensible approximation, so this sub-point is minor polish, not an error.

The page defines an endorsement as "a statement by the head of government, or the governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a qualifying UBI" (app.js:313). The paper says "a governing party's platform" and defines a qualifying UBI as "a universal, unconditional, recurring payment" (index.qmd:86). I fetched Lei 10.835 from planalto.gov.br. It was sanctioned ("eu sanciono") and signed by LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA on 8 January 2004. Art. 1 institutes a benefit for all residents "não importando sua condição socioeconômica", paid annually, and §2 sets it at "igual valor para todos". That is a sitting head of government backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment inside the 2000+ window.

I also fetched Lei 14.601/2023, Art. 1 §1, signed under Lula in the current term. It says Bolsa Família "constitui etapa do processo gradual e progressivo de implementação da universalização da renda básica de cidadania". That is arguably a second event.

Under the "governing party's platform" wording, two more cases in the repo's own ledger qualify on the same logic:
- Korea 2022: Lee was the DP nominee while the DP governed. The KOR govShort and endorseNote say he "pledged a universal payment in 2022", and country_research.json says 1M won per person per year.
- France 2017: Hamon was the PS nominee while the PS governed, running on a universal income (FRA endorseNote and facts). The original finding did not mention this case.

research/prompts/endorse.md pre-labels Korea as "campaign only" and never lists Brazil 2004. That exclusion rule exists only in an internal prompt, not in the published resolution text. The German Greens' "guiding idea" I judge weak: their practical model is means-tested. It does expose a dashboard-versus-paper gap ("the" versus "a" governing party).

2) A careful reader would see the contradiction. In the staged maxghenis.com PR #62 (head 48234513), the Brazil panel of public/ubi-forecast/index.html shows the fact "Law 10.835/2004 ... created a citizen's basic income from 2005" and the L_shock note "A universal statute already exists". As written, the 'Checkable soon' resolution text could count a re-elected Lula government's standing Law 14.601 framing as an endorsement already.

3) Headline impact. This part of the original finding is wrong: the no-shock rates contribute far more than 0.1 points to some headline numbers. The base run reproduced paper/results.json exactly: US 2040 2.49%, any-of-ten 2040 17.80%, US endorse by 2030 2.62%, any-of-ten endorse by 2030 11.74%.

| No-shock rate change | US 2040 | Any-of-ten 2040 | Any-of-ten endorse by 2030 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base (as published) | 2.49% | 17.80% | 11.74% |
| All no-shock rates set to zero | 2.52% | 14.32% | 3.43% |
| L_normal x2 (Brazil 2004 alone, all events left-led) | 2.50% | 19.76% | 17.05% |
| L_normal x2.5 | 2.50% | 20.71% | 19.67% |

The ledger has "If the US trigger is met, {country}'s is met too" and "…and within this many years of the US" (app.js:338-339). The paper says "with a probability conditional on the US trigger" (index.qmd:78). The exposure control offers "The US only" and "Every country, in the same year as the US". What is never stated is the complement: that a country's trigger has zero chance of being met while the US trigger is not. A probability conditional on the US trigger says nothing about that case. - The How text (app.js:373) says "Each other country may meet its own version of the trigger, with its own chance and lag".
- The control default is "Each country's own chance and lag".
- The "Checkable soon" table and the paper's tbl-soon caption say triggers resolve from each country's official series.
Under that resolution rule, any local trigger counts, whatever its cause.

The finding holds, and for a different reason than the finding gives. Line 94 of paper/index.qmd (branch revision-2, HEAD 2b027ba) says: "small without a shock (dividend-scale, like Alaska's)". That is true only for the US prior.

**No-shock amount modes in dashboard/src/countries.js** (% of GDP per head):
- US: 2.22, i.e. `usd(2000)`. Its amountNote says "dividend-scale, around $2,000".
- KOR 2.5, JPN 4, BRA 4.
- AUS 7, GBR 8, CAN 8, DEU 10, ESP 10, FRA 11.

**Engine check.** In engine.js, lines 258 and 286-287, the median is a PERT draw from `c.amount.normal`. The amount is then that median times exp(0.6·z), floored at 1.11. So "a lognormal centered on the country's prior" is accurate, but "dividend-scale" is not. I ran this draw myself for each country. The share of no-shock draws at or above the 6.665% threshold:
- US 4.5%, KOR 10.9%, BRA 25%, JPN 32%
- AUS 55%, GBR 62%, CAN 64%, DEU 75%, ESP 76%, FRA 78%

For six of the ten countries, the typical no-shock UBI clears the paper's $6,000-equivalent bar. That is the opposite of what "dividend-scale" means in a paper whose US story relies on no-shock programs falling below the bar.

**Why major, not blocker.** The error is in how the Methods section describes the inputs. It does not change any computed number. Every headline figure is either US-only or comes from runs using the real inputs. And no-shock endorsement is only about 1% per term everywhere, so few histories take this path. Still, a reader interpreting the non-US or "any of the ten" results would get the wrong idea of the inputs. I found no other copy that repeats the claim: grepping app.js, template.html, results.mjs and build_assets.py turned up no "dividend" or "Alaska" wording. The dashboard row at app.js:359 shows the actual prior ranges.

**The suggested fix is itself partly wrong.** It says the non-US priors "sit near their existing minimum-income benefits (8 to 11%)". But the countries.js amountNotes put those benefits well above the priors: UC 11% against a mode of 8, Bürgergeld 12.5% against 10, RSA 18% against 11, IMV 26% against 10, JobSeeker 21% against 7. Canada has no amountNote at all. The priors sit below those benefits, not near them, and the six countries' range is 7 to 11, not 8 to 11.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real. paper/index.qmd line 94 says the first-year amount is "small without a shock (dividend-scale, like Alaska's)". That is true of only one country's input. In dashboard/src/countries.js the no-shock amount priors (lo/mode/hi, % of GDP per head) are: US 1.11/2.22/3.89 (usd(1000/2000/3500)), KOR 0.5/2.5/7, JPN 1.5/4/13.4, BRA 1.5/4/9, AUS 3/7/14, GBR 4/8/14, CAN 4/8/16, DEU 4/10/22, ESP 4/10/25, FRA 4/11/22. The model's own note calls the US $2,000 (2.2%) "dividend-scale", and the engine counts nothing below 1.11% ($1,000). By that standard, South Korea is also dividend-scale, Japan and Brazil are about twice it, and six countries have modes at or above the 6.665% qualifying bar (3 to 5 times dividend-scale).

engine.js lines 258 and 285-287 confirm how this is used. The no-shock median is a PERT draw from amount.normal, and the amount is lognormal around it with sigma 0.6. So the rest of the sentence ("lognormal centered on the country's prior", "larger during one") is accurate. The error is only the "dividend-scale" description.

Nothing else in the paper lets a reader catch this. tbl-trigger is captioned "Trigger and amount priors by country" but shows only the shock-amount mode. Line 94 is the paper's only description of no-shock amounts. The dashboard is not misleading: app.js line 358 prints each country's no-shock range in the ledger, and I found no "dividend" wording in app.js or template.html. The same sentence is in the staged site build (maxghenis.com PR #62, ref ubi-revision-2, public/ubi-forecast/paper/web/index.html).

Impact, from a real run: I re-ran the engine at the paper's settings (200,000 histories, seed 20260929). The base run reproduces the published numbers exactly: any of ten by 2040 17.80%, by 2050 40.23%, US 2040 2.49%. I then ran a counterfactual where the paper's sentence is literally true, giving every country the US dividend-scale no-shock prior. The results:
- Any of ten by 2040 falls from 17.8% to 14.8%.
- Any of ten by 2050 falls from 40.2% to 36.1%.
- Non-US 2040 figures drop by 0.1 to 0.7 points (for example, AUS 4.61% to 3.91%, GBR 3.09% to 2.78%).
- Each non-US "by 2040 if no AI shock" figure in tbl-countries falls about tenfold (AUS 0.96% to 0.08%, CAN 0.69% to 0.06%, GBR 0.44% to 0.04%).
- The US numbers are unchanged, and any-size numbers are unchanged, as expected.

So the text describes a model whose "any of ten" figure would be about 3 points lower than the published one. It also hides why the non-US no-shock column (0.4 to 1.0%) is 5 to 20 times the US figure (<0.1%). A careful reader of the paper would be misled about a stated assumption, which matters given the owner's goal that assumptions be stated and falsifiable.

It is not a blocker. No computed number is wrong. The US headline and every published figure come from the actual inputs. It is one sentence of methods description, and the dashboard ledger shows the true inputs. It fits the rubric's "major": a wrong claim that should be fixed before publishing but does not change a headline number. The fix is a text edit, not a model change, unless the owner actually intends dividend-scale no-shock amounts everywhere. In that case the inputs, and the 17.8%/40% figures, would change.

findings.decision_impact: This misstates what a headline number means on the paper's landing page and in link previews. The fix is a one-line copy change.

votes.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The main claim holds. The wrapper description says "It puts a US UBI worth $6,000 a year at 2.5% by 2040 ... and 17.8% that at least one of the ten enacts one by 2040." Here "one" can only mean "a UBI worth $6,000 a year".

The model does not compute that. In engine.js, THRESHOLDS = [1.11, 2.5, 6.665, 15, 25] are percentages of each country's own GDP per head. Line 297 records firstYear when x.amount >= THRESHOLDS[t], and x.amount is also a percentage of GDP per head (lines 258-287). results.mjs builds sets.all from at(base, ALL, t, y), and build_assets.py maps sets.all[2] to all_t2_*. In paper/results.json, sets.all[2]["2040"] = 0.17798, so all_t2_2040 = 17.8% is the event "any of the ten enacts at least 6.665% of its own 2025 GDP per head".

Using the gdppc values in countries.js, I computed that bar in dollars: USA $6,000, GBR $3,839, CAN $3,712, DEU $4,032, FRA $3,265, ESP $2,574, JPN $2,396, KOR $2,415, AUS $4,341, BRA $714. For nine of the ten countries the bar is well below $6,000, so the wrapper overstates what the 17.8% means.

This is not handled anywhere else on the wrapper page. The manuscript abstract (paper/index.qmd:8) adds "(6.7% of GDP per head)", but the wrapper omits it. The staged page in maxghenis.com PR #62 (branch ubi-revision-2) is public/ubi-forecast/paper/index.html. It carries the phrase three times: meta description, og:description and the visible paper-desc paragraph. The text outside the iframe never mentions "GDP per head". So the misreading reaches link previews and the landing text as written.

The dashboard does not have this problem. When more than one country is selected, app.js:255 and shareLabel label the threshold as "% of GDP per head", not dollars.

The second sub-claim, that the $6,000 conversion at 2025 GDP per head is "unstated", is overstated for the paper. paper/index.qmd:64 says the 6.7% default "equals $6,000 a year in the United States, whose 2025 GDP per head was {{gdppc_usa}}". It is unstated only on the wrapper, and that part is minor on its own.

Severity: the 17.8% number itself is correct and the manuscript describes it correctly, so no headline number changes. But the landing page and link-preview description misstate what that secondary headline measures. That fits major, near the blocker line because link previews travel without the manuscript.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real. The wrapper description in paper/scripts/build_wrapper.py lines 16-21 is used three times: meta description, og:description and the visible paper-desc paragraph. It says "It puts a US UBI worth $6,000 a year at 2.5% by 2040 ... and 17.8% that at least one of the ten enacts one by 2040." The same text is in the staged output in maxghenis.com PR #62 (head 48234513).

The 17.8% is all_t2_2040, which comes from out.sets.all[2][2040] in results.mjs. That is threshold index 2 of THRESHOLDS = [1.11, 2.5, 6.665, 15, 25] (engine.js line 20). The engine compares each country's amount, in % of its own GDP per head, against that threshold (engine.js line 297). So the bar is 6.665% of each country's own GDP per head. At 2025 World Bank NY.GDP.PCAP.CD values that is $6,000 in the US, $3,839 in the UK, $3,265 in France, $2,574 in Spain, $2,396 in Japan, $2,415 in South Korea and $714 in Brazil.

No reading of "enacts one" makes 17.8% true:
- **"One" means a UBI worth $6,000 a year.** I ran the model's own engine with per-country $6,000 thresholds added: same seed and history count, same draws. That gives 12.7% by 2040 (32.0% by 2050), not 17.8%. The run reproduced 17.80% and 2.49% for the unmodified thresholds, so the draws match. Japan drops from 1.35% to 0.20%, Korea from 1.33% to 0.11%, Brazil from 0.52% to 0.00%.
- **"One" means a UBI of any size.** The model's figure is all_any_2040 = 23.7%.

So the wrapper, which is also the link-preview text, states something false by about 5 points (a 40% relative overstatement) under its plain reading.

Why major rather than blocker:
- The number 17.8% is a correct model output. Only its label is wrong, and correcting the label changes no published number.
- The manuscript embedded directly below gets it right. The abstract adds "(6.7% of GDP per head)", and index.qmd line 64 says the threshold is a share of GDP per head equal to $6,000 in the US at 2025 GDP per head. Line 132 uses the figure correctly.
- The dashboard labels multi-country thresholds as a share of GDP per head (app.js line 255), and its meta and og descriptions contain no such claim.

A careful reader of the paper is not misled. A reader who sees only the link preview or the wrapper paragraph is, and that is the most-shared text, so this is at the top of major and must be fixed before publishing.

The second sub-point is minor. Every "$6,000" label converts at 2025 GDP per head, and the bar in dollars rises with GDP per head. But index.qmd line 64 states the 2025 basis and that the threshold is a share of GDP per head. Only the wrapper and the dashboard's single-country dollar labels omit it.

votes.reasoning:
Both parts of the claim hold up, and the wording is also in the page staged for publish and on the live page.

(1) "Every assumption adjustable" is false. The only controls are:
- c-shift (moves the trigger date)
- c-exposure (three modes)
- four multipliers: eL, eR, pass and amt
- four risk toggles: fiscal, meansTested, diffusion and gridlock

In engine.js:247-259 the multipliers apply as flat factors to every country: ctl.endorse[type], ctl.pass and ctl.amount, and the O multiplier is the average of eL and eR (app.js controlsFrom). These inputs have no control:
- election pL/pR
- midterm keep
- per-country exposure probability and lag (only overridden wholesale by the "all" or "us-only" modes)
- ratchet
- politics_lag_years
- the level of the shock_by_* probabilities (the shift moves timing only)
- relative per-country values
- a separate O-type endorsement multiplier and per-type passage

The page's own copy contradicts the meta tag. The control panel says "Each slider scales every country's explicit value by the same factor". The paper's Fig 1 caption (index.qmd:70) says a "dashed box marks where the dashboard's sliders and risk switches act", i.e. on a subset.

(2) "Every input sourced", and the ledger lede defining judgment as "an estimate from the evidence listed", are not supported for many rows. I mirrored renderAssumptions against countries.js with all ten countries. 72 per-country rows get the "judgment" badge with an empty Basis note:
- endorse R_shock ×10, O_shock ×10
- pass R ×10, O ×10
- no-shock amount ×10
- ratchet ×10
- lag ×9
- exposure ×2 (FRA and AUS, which have no exposureNote)
- CAN shock amount ×1 (no amountNote)

The denominator of 138 is the exposure, lag, endorse, pass, amount and ratchet rows, excluding trigger and period rows. With those included there are 225 rows, 161 of them judgment.

A few of these rows get some cover from sibling-row notes or the country facts list. The US amountNote mentions the no-shock amount, and the GBR endorseNote mentions Reform and the Conservatives. Ratchet (a flat 5-25%, mode 12%, for every country) and lag have no stated basis anywhere on the page. The word "ratchet" does not appear in paper/index.qmd either.

Why major and not blocker: no number changes, and the page body describes the sliders accurately. But the meta description and link-preview text make a false public claim that directly cuts against the owner's falsifiability goal. It is not new in rev 2: origin/main and the live rev-1 page carry it too, so publishing rev 2 as staged repeats it.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and a second problem sits on the same link-preview surface.

1. "Every assumption adjustable" is false. The page has six controls and four risk switches. The shift slider (-5..10) moves trigger dates but does not change the shock_by_* probabilities. The exposure dropdown offers model, all or us-only. Four sliders (eL, eR, pass, amt; app.js:30, :59-62) scale every country's values by one shared factor. In engine.js:230-262, these inputs have no control:
- election and midterm probabilities, and politics_lag_years
- each country's exposure probability and lag (only overridden to 1/0, and lag to 0, by the dropdown)
- ratchet
- the amount dispersion constants (0.5/0.6)
- the per-country relative values
The O endorsement multiplier is tied to the average of L and R, and one slider scales both the shock and no-shock endorsement rates. One nuance: the finding says exposure "cannot be adjusted", but the dropdown does give two coarse overrides.

2. "Every input sourced" and the ledger lede ("judgment: an estimate from the evidence listed") fail on the page's own ledger. I copied the renderAssumptions logic (app.js:325-366) into a script run against countries.js and got the finding's number exactly: 72 per-country rows are labeled judgment with an empty Basis. They are:
- endorse R_shock and O_shock (10 each)
- pass R and O (10 each)
- amount normal (10)
- ratchet (10)
- lag (9)
- exposure (2)
- amount shock (1)
The finding's denominator of 138 is the non-period, non-trigger rows (148 − 10). Another 20 rows labeled data (R_normal and O_normal) also have an empty Basis. For some of these rows a neighbouring row's note partly covers them: endorseBaseNote sits on L_normal, passNote on L, and amountNote on the shock row. Ratchet (one shared RATCHET constant) and lag have no evidence anywhere in the ledger.

3. Scope: the paper does not repeat the overclaim. Its Fig. 1 caption says the dashed box marks where the sliders act. The page body's slider help is also accurate ("Each slider scales every country's explicit value by the same factor"). So the false wording is in the search and preview metadata, the OG image caption, and the ledger lede. No number changes.

Severity: major, at the low end. It does not change a headline number. But it is a false statement about how the dashboard works, placed on its most widely seen surface (search snippet, social preview). The "every input sourced" and "evidence listed" wording directly undercuts revision 2's stated goal: a careful reader who follows the ledger lede to the ratchet or lag rows finds nothing listed. The fix is a few lines of copy.

Adjacent issue, found while checking this and not part of the finding. I rate it blocker-class for link previews. The og:image and twitter:image both point to https://maxghenis.com/ubi-forecast/og-image.png. The image is built from dashboard/og/og.html, which hard-codes "9.6%" (revision 1) and "Every assumption adjustable." maxghenis.com PR #62 does not touch og-image.png. Its file list is index.html, the paper files and vercel.json. On branch ubi-revision-2, og-image.png has blob sha 7e5a4754…, identical to the repo's image and byte-identical (shasum) to the live one. After publishing, every social or Slack preview of the revision-2 page would therefore show "$6,000 a year… 2040… 9.6%", while the page says 2.5%.

reviewed.summary:
I checked all 29 cited works, including the 12 marked pending. None is fabricated. Bibliographic metadata is correct for every entry: 26 were checked against Crossref by DOI, plus spot checks of JAIR's Article 9, NBER's August 2026 revision date, and Kangas's chapter 14, pp. 187-196. Of the 12 pending references, 11 support the sentences that cite them; the exception is verho2022removing.

- **Blocker (misattribution):** index.qmd:120 says "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]." Verho et al. report no detectable first-year employment effect, and they say the second-year gain cannot be attributed to the experiment alone. The paper reports no wellbeing outcome at all. The same sentence is in the staged maxghenis.com PR #62 paper. The fix is one sentence (cite Kangas 2021 for wellbeing), and no number changes.
- **Minor issues:**
  - The De Wispelaere-Noguera mapping (index.qmd:88) is loose: passage is mainly strategic feasibility, and institutional feasibility is about implementation.
  - Banerjee et al. is cited for an advanced-country fiscal claim, but it covers developing countries only.
  - "Modest" understates the August 2026 Vivalt revision; the authors call the effect "moderate", with participation down 4.2 points.
  - The file listing references as pending verification is stale, and there is an unused duplicate bib file.

Everything else checked out, including the IMF 60% figure, the 208 NFL games, Grace et al.'s 2116 date, Acemoglu's 0.66%, and the ESS support range of about a third to four-fifths. Once the Verho sentence is fixed, the citations do not stand in the way of publishing.

Metadata for all 26 DOI-bearing entries matches Crossref: authors, title, venue, volume, issue, pages and year (scratchpad crossref.py, crossref.json). Crossref's 'De / Wispelaere' name split is a Crossref quirk; the bib is correct.

findings.claim: "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]"
findings.evidence: The AEJ:Policy abstract, which I read on aeaweb.org and in OpenAlex, says the reform "has minor employment effects at best" and "days in employment remained statistically unchanged in the first year of the experiment." The VATT WP 142 full text (doria.fi PDF, pdftotext) gives the main finding as "no detectable employment effect in the first year" (1.5 days, 95% CI -2.3 to 5.4). The second-year +6.6 days "cannot be attributed to the basic income experiment alone" because the 2018 activation reform coincided with it, and the authors "focus primarily on the first-year result." Grepping the full text for well-being/wellbeing finds only a mention of Haushofer and Shapiro's Kenya study. The paper reports no wellbeing outcome for Finland. Kangas (2021, ch. 14, p.193, read from the utupub.fi PDF) says recipients "did not work significantly more or less than the control population." The wellbeing gains Kangas mentions come from chapters 7, 8 and 10 of that book, not from Verho et al. The same sentence appears in the rendered paper/index.html and index.pdf, and in the staged maxghenis.com PR #62 file public/ubi-forecast/paper/web/index.html at the PR head (grep count 1).
findings.fix: Replace with: "Finland's experiment had no detectable effect on employment in its first year [@verho2022removing], though recipients reported better wellbeing [@kangas2021feasibility]". Kangas ch. 14 p.193 supports the wellbeing clause; alternatively add a bib entry for the book's wellbeing chapter 7.
findings.decision_impact: This sentence attributes a finding to a paper that does not report it, and it reverses that paper's headline employment result. Under this review's rule (misattributed = blocker) it should be fixed before the paper goes live. The fix is one sentence, and no model number depends on it.

votes.reasoning:
The misattribution holds up. paper/index.qmd:120 cites only [@verho2022removing] for "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing". That paper does not support either clause as written.

(1) Employment. The paper's abstract (from OpenAlex, and the same in the VATT WP 142 text) says the reform "has minor employment effects at best". It also says days in employment "remained statistically unchanged in the first year". The conclusion (VATT WP 142, around line 991) gives the "main finding" as "no detectable employment effect in the first year" (1.5 days, 95% CI -2.3 to 5.4). The second-year estimate of 6.6 days (CI 1.3 to 11.9) coincides with the 2018 reform, so it "cannot be attributed to the basic income experiment alone". For that reason the authors "focus primarily on the first-year result". Saying the paper found that the experiment "raised employment" reverses its stated headline.

(2) Wellbeing. The only wellbeing mention in the full text is Haushofer and Shapiro's Kenya study (line 151). The paper uses administrative employment data and reports no wellbeing outcome for Finland.

(3) The project's own research/citations_raw.json summarizes Verho correctly ("Days in employment were statistically unchanged in the first year ... minor employment effects at best"), so the manuscript contradicts its own notes. The sentence is also in the rendered paper/index.html and index.pdf (grep count 1 each), and in the staged maxghenis.com PR #62 file public/ubi-forecast/paper/web/index.html at head 48234513 (fetched via gh api).

Why major and not blocker: the task rubric reserves blocker for text that states something false or materially misleading about the world, or a bug that moves a headline number. As a claim about the Finnish experiment, the sentence matches the official evaluation's own summary. VATT's press release is titled "small employment effects, better perceived economic security and mental wellbeing". It reports +6 days of employment from Nov 2017 to Oct 2018, with the caveat that the second-year effect cannot be separated from the activation model, and better wellbeing from a Kela survey. So readers do not get a false picture of Finland. They get a citation that misstates what Verho et al. found, and it drops the confounding caveat. That is a wrong, unsupported attribution that should be fixed before publishing. No model input or headline number depends on it: a grep of dashboard/src finds no Finland or Verho reference, and the sentence itself says effects evidence "enters only through feasibility". The finder rated it a blocker under a citation-dimension rule that misattribution is a blocker. The task's own rubric puts this at major.

Side note: paper/references_PENDING_VERIFICATION.txt still lists verho2022removing and kangas2021feasibility as awaiting the verifier job, while citations_raw.json marks both verified: True.
