votes.better_fix: Split the attribution and keep the confounding caveat. Suggested wording: "Finland's experiment had no detectable effect on employment in its first year [@verho2022removing]; recipients worked about six more days over the full period, a gain its evaluators could not separate from a 2018 activation reform, and reported better wellbeing [@<final-evaluation cite>]." For the second cite, add a bib entry for the edited volume (Kangas, Jauhiainen, Simanainen and Ylikännö, eds., 2021, Experimenting with Unconditional Basic Income, Edward Elgar, doi 10.4337/9781839104855), or for its wellbeing and employment chapters. Do not lean on ch. 14 (kangas2021feasibility): it is a feasibility chapter, and I could not verify the p.193 wording it would rest on. Verify the new cite's page or chapter against the open-access text before publishing. Re-render the paper and restage PR #62. Also clear verho2022removing and kangas2021feasibility from references_PENDING_VERIFICATION.txt only once the verifier job actually runs.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and both halves of the attribution are wrong.

1. Employment. paper/index.qmd line 120 says "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]". The Verho et al. abstract says the reform "has minor employment effects at best" and that days in employment "remained statistically unchanged in the first year". The VATT WP 142 full text gives the main finding as no detectable first-year employment effect: 1.5 days, 95% CI -2.3 to 5.4. The second-year estimate is 6.6 days, but the authors say it "cannot be attributed to the basic income experiment alone" because of the 2018 unemployment benefit reform, so they focus on the first year. "Raised employment slightly" can only be read out of that confounded second-year number, and the authors explicitly disclaim it. So the sentence turns the paper's headline null into a positive effect.

2. Wellbeing. The WP text mentions well-being only once, when it describes Haushofer and Shapiro's Kenya study. Verho et al. report no wellbeing outcome for Finland.

3. The project's own notes contradict the sentence. In research/citations_raw.json, the "supports" note for verho2022removing says days in employment were statistically unchanged and the effects were "minor employment effects at best". paper/references_PENDING_VERIFICATION.txt lists verho2022removing and kangas2021feasibility as still awaiting the citation verifier. The prose drifted from a correct source note and was never checked.

4. The fix the finding proposes is supported. I downloaded Kangas ch. 14 from utupub.fi. It says recipients "did not work significantly more or less than the control population". It also says basic income was "positively and significantly associated with improvements in Finns' mental and social well-being", citing the book's Chapter 7. So kangas2021feasibility, which is already in the bib, can carry the wellbeing clause.

Why major and not blocker:
- No model input, dashboard number or headline depends on this sentence. The paragraph itself says "Evidence on effects enters only through feasibility". The dashboard source (app.js, template.html, countries.js) never mentions Finland or Verho.
- The error sits in background literature, not in the forecast or its assumptions. It does not change what a reader should believe about the probabilities.
- It is still a clear misattributed citation in a public working paper, and it errs in the pro-UBI direction. That is a credibility problem for a forecasting paper, and a referee or a Finland-literate reader would catch it quickly.

That matches this review's definition of major exactly: "a wrong or unsupported claim that should be fixed before publishing but does not change the headline". I would not hold publication beyond the time it takes to fix this one sentence, but it should be fixed before PR #62 goes live. If the owner applies a strict "any misattribution is a blocker" rule, the finding's original label is also defensible. The difference is only whether it gates publication; the one-sentence fix is the same either way.

findings.claim: "The steps also map onto the political-feasibility framework of @dewispelaere2012feasibility: endorsement captures strategic feasibility among governing actors, and passage captures institutional feasibility."
findings.evidence: I could not read the primary chapter; Springer requires a login. Two descriptions of the framework do not match this mapping. First, Kangas (2021, p.189-190), citing De Wispelaere and Noguera 2012 pp.24-7, writes that institutional feasibility "refers to the administrative challenges posed by the implementation of a policy ... updated citizen registers, implementing new payment tools, and monitoring payment of benefits." Under strategic feasibility, Kangas writes "For major social policy reform to pass, it must be supported by a robust coalition of political parties and social partners." Second, co-author Noguera, interviewed at praktykateoretyczna.pl, says strategic feasibility "has to do with the relations of power in a given political context to get support for basic income" and institutional feasibility with "how basic income fits within given welfare institutions". His examples are pension compatibility and regional competences. So passage is mainly strategic feasibility, and institutional feasibility is about implementation and institutional fit. That fit can block passage, so the mapping is partly defensible, but it is not the framework's own split.
findings.fix: Rephrase: "Both steps test what @dewispelaere2012feasibility call strategic feasibility, whether governing actors will build and use a coalition; passage also absorbs institutional feasibility, whether existing institutions allow a UBI to be implemented."
findings.decision_impact: An interpretive simplification that a referee who knows the framework would flag. It changes no number and does not need to hold publication, but it is a one-line fix.

findings.claim: "None of these settles the fiscal question that dominates political debate in advanced countries [@hoynes2019universal; @banerjee2019universal; @kangas2021feasibility]."
findings.evidence: The Banerjee, Niehaus and Suri abstract (OpenAlex) and the NBER w25598 full text concern developing countries only. Page 2 hands advanced-country issues to Hoynes and Rothstein. Its fiscal discussion covers low-income countries ("funding anything close to a UBI would require a substantial share of available resources") and argues the "costs" of UBI are "relatively low" there. The sentence is supported by Hoynes and Rothstein ("A UBI large enough to increase transfers to low-income families would be enormously expensive"; pilots "will do little to resolve the major outstanding questions"). It is also supported by Kangas p.191: support falls to about 30% when taxes are mentioned, and a UBI is unlikely to be financeable "with increases in income tax alone".
findings.fix: Remove @banerjee2019universal from this bracket, or add a clause such as "...in advanced countries [@hoynes2019universal; @kangas2021feasibility] or poorer ones [@banerjee2019universal]".
findings.decision_impact: A tangential citation, not a false one. It is polish and does not block publishing.

findings.claim: "the OpenResearch trial found modest reductions in work [@vivalt2024employment]"
findings.evidence: The NBER w32719 page, downloaded with curl, shows "Revision Date August 2026". Its abstract now reports "a 4.2 percentage point decrease in labor market participation", work hours down "by 1-2 hours/week", and partners reducing hours "by a comparable amount". It concludes: "our results suggest a moderate labor supply effect that does not appear offset by other productive activities." "Modest" understates the authors' own word, "moderate", in the revision the bib entry cites (note = Revised August 2026).
findings.fix: Use the authors' word: "the OpenResearch trial found moderate reductions in work (labor-force participation down 4.2 points) [@vivalt2024employment]".
findings.decision_impact: Wording polish that does not block publishing.

reviewed.summary:
This review tested the claim behind revision 2's no-shock endorsement prior: that none of the ten governments endorsed a strict UBI in about 75 government terms since 2000. Under the model's own definition of an endorsement, the claim is false.

**Counterexamples found:**
- **Brazil 2004 (clear).** Lula signed Law 10.835, a universal, unconditional, equal, annual payment, and said it 'faz parte da política social que o governo quer implementar'.
- **South Korea 2022 (strong).** The governing Democratic Party registered a universal basic income (250,000 won a year rising to 1 million) among its 10 main pledges with the National Election Commission.
- **Brazil 2023 (arguable).** The 2022 Lula–Alckmin platform, and Lei 14.601 §1 signed by Lula, name a universal basic citizenship income as the goal.
- The dashboard's own Brazil note and the project's research files already record the Brazilian items.

**Korea today.** Lee's government is not clearly an endorser yet, but the resolution rule cannot decide. The health ministry told the Cabinet in May 2026 that it would pursue introducing a basic income. In June 2026 Lee told The Economist that 'a new mechanism such as basic income payments will be needed', with hedges. If these count, the model's un-endorsed start is wrong. Korea's chance of a UBI of any size by 2040 would go from 4.1% to 50.8%, and at-least-one-of-ten by 2040 from 17.8% to 22.5% (scratch run).

**The count and the arithmetic.**
- 'About 75' matches elections held since 2000.
- The 47%/11% pair fits no single N: at N=75 the 3% case gives 10%.
- In the model's own per-term units the exposure is 66 terms, giving 51% and 13%.
- For left-led governments, the only type L_normal applies to (about 22 term-equivalents), even a clean record favours 1% over 3% by only 1.5 to 1. 'Rules out' is not supported.
- Once the counterexamples are counted, the record favours higher left-led rates: 3% is favoured 2 to 18 times over 1%, and the maximum-likelihood rate is 5–14% per term.

**Effect on the numbers.** Raising L_normal accordingly barely moves the US headline (2.49% to 2.51–2.54%). It raises at-least-one-of-ten by 2040 (17.8% to 21–25%) and any-of-ten endorsing by 2030 (11.7% to 18–27%).

**Revision note.** The claim that the record-based recalibration helped lower the US forecast from 9.6% is contradicted by a run: putting revision 1's no-shock rates back moves the US 2040 figure only from 2.49% to 2.52%.

**Recommendation:** publish the US headline if you want, but not this sentence or the non-US endorsement numbers as they stand. Before publishing:
- rewrite the record claim in all 14 places it appears;
- adopt one resolution rule covering amounts, junior coalition partners, convention resolutions, candidate platforms, standing laws and endorsements made before 2027;
- settle Korea's and Brazil's starting states;
- recalibrate L_normal or relabel it as judgment, then rerun results.mjs.

Scratch scripts and outputs are under /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-review/record/: recompute.py (the arithmetic), eng/run.mjs and eng/out.json (engine variants), eng/run2.mjs (the revision-1 rates test), and eng/engine.js (a scratch copy of the engine with a start-endorsed option).
checked: My scratch copy of dashboard/src/engine.js (200,000 histories, seed 20260929) reproduces the published baseline: US $6k by 2040 2.49%, US by 2050 7.43%, at-least-one-of-ten 17.80%, US with no trigger 0.01% (<0.1%), US endorses by 2030 2.62%, any of ten endorses by 2030 11.74%, Korea endorses by 2028 1.39% and by 2030 2.94%, Brazil 0.37% and 0.79%. These match paper/_variables.yml and table_soon.md.

'About 75' matches the count of general elections and presidential terms that started from 2000 to 2026: US 7, UK 7, Canada 9, Germany 7, France 5, Spain 9, Japan 10, Korea 6, Australia 9, Brazil 6. I counted these from my own knowledge and did not web-verify them this session; only the arithmetic was executed. 0.99^75 = 0.4706 checks out as 47%.

Brazil's STF MI 7300 (2021) was a court order to start the law's first phase for the poor, not a government endorsement (CNM and Conjur summaries). EC 114/2021's constitutional 'renda básica familiar' is targeted: I read 'Todo brasileiro em situação de vulnerabilidade social' on planalto.gov.br.
Brazil 2026: Lula's platform dropped the basic-citizenship-income language (Gazeta do Povo, 17 Aug 2026). This is consistent with the countries.js fact about the 2026 platforms.
Korea's DP platform (강령, Dec 2025 PDF from theminjoo.kr, 15,584 lines after pdftotext) has no instance of 기본소득; it has 기본사회 and 보편적 기본서비스. The platform itself is therefore not an endorsement.

Korea's 2027 health-ministry pilot is a participation income for young and middle-aged adults, not a universal payment (Asiae, April 2026). This is consistent with the model not treating it as a qualifying program.
Spain's 2023 PSOE-Sumar agreement strengthens the means-tested IMV and revises child benefits; I found no basic income in it (Eduardo Rojo's transcription). This supports the Spain note.
Japan: Ishin's 2026 platform proposes a menu (refundable credit, negative income tax or basic income), not a UBI. This supports the Japan note.
Germany: the Greens' programme treats an unconditional basic income as a guiding idea, while their Garantiesicherung is means-tested. This supports the Germany note's 'guiding idea' wording.
France: Hamon's final 2017 plan was income-tested (Institut Montaigne summary), and he was not in government. This supports the France note.
UK: I found no statement by Burnham as Prime Minister backing a UBI through September 2026 (Big Issue, 22 Jul 2026; Labour conference coverage, 26-27 Sep 2026). This supports the UK note.
The US and Australia were not researched this session beyond the repo's notes.
The engine's lapse rule (engine.js:276) and un-endorsed start (engine.js:262) match the rule described in the paper and dashboard.

findings.claim: "None of the ten governments endorsed a strict UBI in about 75 government terms since 2000, so no-shock endorsement is near 1% per term." The same text appears in all ten ledger notes (countries.js lines 47, 97, 135, 169, 204, 238, 274, 307, 347, 382), in app.js:379, index.qmd:186, model/ubi_model.py:100 and model/inputs.json:91. It is labeled source "data" and sets L_normal to PERT(0.002, 0.01, 0.03).
findings.evidence:
The model defines an endorsement as "a statement by the head of government, or a governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment" (index.qmd:86). Under that definition the record has counterexamples.
(a) Brazil, Lula's first term, 2003-06, left-led. I fetched Law 10.835 of 8 Jan 2004 from planalto.gov.br. Art. 1 grants every Brazilian resident 'não importando sua condição socioeconômica, receberem, anualmente, um benefício monetário'. §2 says 'de igual valor para todos', and §3 allows monthly payments. The law is signed 'LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA'. Conjur (8 Jan 2004) quotes Lula at the signing: the law 'faz parte da política social que o governo quer implementar'. This is a clear endorsement under the definition.
(b) South Korea, February 2022, Moon presidency with a DP majority, left-led. Kyunghyang (11 Feb 2022) reports that the DP election committee submitted its 10 main pledges to the National Election Commission on 10 Feb. They include a universal basic income that 'starts at 250,000 won a year and grows to 1 million won within the term' (Seoul Shinmun: '전 국민 보편기본소득'). The DP was then the governing party, with 172 seats (Kyunghyang editorial, 10 Mar 2022). The model itself says Lee 'pledged a universal payment in 2022' (countries.js:308).
(c) Brazil, Lula's third term, 2023-26. This one is arguable. Lei 14.601/2023 Art. 1 §1, signed by Lula, says Bolsa Família 'constitui etapa do processo gradual e progressivo de implementação da universalização da renda básica de cidadania'. The 2022 Lula-Alckmin programme (pdftotext, item 20) says Bolsa Família 'viabilizará a transição por etapas, no rumo de um sistema universal e uma renda básica de cidadania'.
The dashboard's own Brazil note (countries.js:283) and research/country_research.json record both Brazilian items. 'Strict UBI' is defined nowhere in the repo. research/prompts/endorse.md told the researcher to treat Lee's 2022 pledge as 'campaign only'.
Effect on outputs: I ran a scratch copy of engine.js with 200,000 histories and seed 20260929. It reproduces the published baseline exactly. Changing L_normal for all ten countries to R(0.01, 0.03, 0.08) moves at-least-one-of-ten at 6.7% by 2040 from 17.80% to 21.22%, and any-of-ten endorsing by 2030 from 11.74% to 18.38%. With R(0.02, 0.06, 0.12) those become 25.34% and 27.47%. The US 2040 figure moves only from 2.49% to 2.51% and 2.54%.
findings.fix:
1. Rewrite the sentence everywhere it appears. For example: 'Since 2000, a head of government (Lula, 2004) signed a universal basic income law, and a governing party (Korea's DP, 2022) registered a universal payment as a pledge; none was funded.'
2. Recount endorsements and exposure by government type.
3. Recalibrate L_normal from that count, or label it as judgment. The prior's upper bound of 3% sits below the maximum-likelihood estimate once k ≥ 1.
4. Update ubi_model.py:100, inputs.json:91, app.js:379 and index.qmd:186, then rerun paper/scripts/results.mjs.
findings.decision_impact: Do not publish as-is. The page states as data a fact that its own Brazil ledger row contradicts. Correcting it raises the non-US headlines (17.8% and 11.7%). The US headline of 2.5% barely moves.

findings.claim: The Korea note says Lee pledged a universal payment in 2022 'then dropped it in 2025'. The engine starts every country un-endorsed in 2027 (engine.js:262). With Korea's left-led government fixed for 2027, the model gives 1.4% that a Korean government endorses by 2028 and 2.9% by 2030. The paper calls endorsements 'the sharpest test' (index.qmd:164).
findings.evidence:
1. On 26 May 2026 the health ministry reported the revised 3rd Social Security Basic Plan to the Cabinet. It says: '노동시장 변화와 소득 양극화에 대응하기 위한 새로운 사회안전망으로의 기본소득 도입을 검토·추진한다' (it will review and pursue introducing basic income as a new safety net against labour-market change and income polarization). Source: Maeil Business via Nate.
2. On 10 June 2026 Lee told The Economist that funding a basic income from part of AI excess profits 'could be one of the very useful policy alternatives' (Seoul Shinmun quote: '매우 유용한 정책 대안 중 하나가 될 수 있다'). HuffPost Korea quotes him: '기본소득 지급과 같은 새로운 메커니즘이 필요할 것' (a new mechanism such as basic income payments will be needed). The Presidential Office framed this as 'an era-defining challenge that may be faced someday' (SEDaily).
3. The paper calls Lee 'the most prominent basic-income advocate among heads of government' (index.qmd:38).
4. The ministry's 2027 pilot is a participation income, not a universal payment (Asiae, April 2026).
5. The DP platform (Dec 2025 PDF) contains no instance of 기본소득; it has only 기본사회 (basic society).
Under a strict reading this is not yet an endorsement, but the resolution rule cannot decide it. I patched a scratch engine so that Korea starts 2027 already endorsed. Korea's chance of a UBI of any size by 2040 then rises from 4.08% to 50.81%. At 6.7% of GDP per head it rises from 1.33% to 7.30%. At-least-one-of-ten at 6.7% by 2040 rises from 17.80% to 22.52%, and any size by 2030 from 1.92% to 46.77%.
findings.fix:
1. Add the May and June 2026 facts to the Korea note.
2. Say explicitly whether a hedged statement by a head of government counts. One option: require a concrete universal, unconditional, recurring cash payment to all adults with an amount or a timeline, or a bill or budget line.
3. If such statements count, start Korea endorsed. Then reconcile that with Korea's left-led passage prior of 0.5-0.9 per term, which would turn the standing endorsement into a roughly 50% chance of a UBI by 2040.
findings.decision_impact: A reader can score the Korea 'Checkable soon' row on statements that already exist. This must be settled before publishing. If the owner decides these statements count, it becomes a headline-changing blocker.

findings.claim: 'With that rate the clean record had about a 47% chance, against 11% under a 3% rate.' The revision text (app.js:379, index.qmd:186) adds that 'the record rules out the no-shock rates revision 1 implied'.
findings.evidence:
From recompute.py:
- 0.99^75 = 0.4706 (47%) but 0.97^75 = 0.1018 (10%). No single N gives both figures: 47% needs N = 75-76 and 11% needs N = 72-73.
- The model states rates per term of termYears and converts them to yearly hazards (engine.js:122). In those units, 26.75 years since 2000 is 66.4 terms across the ten countries, which gives 51% and 13%.
- L_normal applies only to left-led governments. By my reading of the type definitions, that is about 21.7 terms since 2000. On those terms a clean record has probability 80.5% at 1% and 52.2% at 3%. That is a likelihood ratio of 1.54, not about 4.6.
- Under the model's own modes (left-led 1%, right-led and other 0.4%), P(clean) = 67%. Integrated over the PERT prior, the chance of no left-led endorsement is 77%.
- Even taken at face value, a ratio of about 4.6 does not 'rule out' 3%.
- With k left-led endorsements on record, the ratio favours 3% over 1% by 1.95 (k=1), 5.8 (k=2) or 17.5 (k=3). The maximum-likelihood rates are 4.6%, 9.2% and 13.9%.
findings.fix:
1. Compute the likelihood in the model's own units, by government type.
2. Report the likelihood ratio and drop 'rules out'.
3. Correct 11% to 10%, or state the N used.
findings.decision_impact: This overstates the evidence for a prior labeled 'data'. Fix before publishing. It does not change the US headline.

findings.claim: Revision 2 'puts it lower, because endorsing first and passing later takes time, an endorsement lapses when the government changes, and the record rules out the no-shock rates revision 1 implied' (also index.qmd:186).
findings.evidence: run2.mjs uses 200,000 histories and the published seed. It sets the US no-shock endorsement rates to revision 1's no-shock values, read with `git show a534969:dashboard/src/countries.js`: L R(0.01, 0.03, 0.07), R R(0.005, 0.02, 0.05), O R(0, 0.003, 0.01). The US chance of $6k by 2040 moves only from 2.49% to 2.52%, and any size from 3.48% to 3.77%. So the no-shock recalibration explains about 0.03 of the 7-point drop from 9.6% to 2.5%.
findings.fix: Drop the third reason, or publish a decomposition of the drop from 9.6% to 2.5% by change, computed from real runs.
findings.decision_impact: This is a mechanism claim in public copy that my run contradicts. Fix before publishing. The headline is unchanged.

findings.claim: 'An endorsement means a statement by the head of government, or a governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment.' The dashboard instead says 'backing a qualifying UBI' (app.js:313), and the base-rate claim uses 'strict UBI'.
findings.evidence:
The three wordings differ. The paper's has no amount and no all-adults requirement, and 'strict' is defined nowhere (grep). The rule leaves open exactly the cases I found this session:
- Junior coalition partners. Movimiento Sumar's November 2025 conference resolution proposes a universal €550 a month for 18- to 21-year-olds as a 'punto de partida' toward income for everyone (Infobae). The German Greens' programme says 'Dabei orientieren wir uns an der Leitidee eines Bedingungslosen Grundeinkommens', but their concrete Garantiesicherung is means-tested. Ishin's 2026 platform proposes '最低所得保障制度（給付付き税額控除、負の所得税またはベーシックインカム）を導入'.
- Party convention resolutions. CBC (10 Apr 2021): delegates of the governing Liberals 'overwhelmingly endorsed a resolution calling for the establishment of a universal basic income (UBI)'.
- Platforms of the incumbent party's candidate. Korea 2022; France 2017, where Hamon's final plan was income-tested (Institut Montaigne summary).
- Standing statutes. Brazil's Law 10.835 and Lei 14.601 §1.
- Endorsements made before 2027, and whether they set the model's starting state.
index.qmd:88 also says 'Endorsements happen far more often than enactments', which contradicts a claimed record of zero endorsements.
findings.fix:
1. Adopt one resolution rule in the paper, the dashboard and the base-rate count. Cover amount, all adults versus age bands, junior partners, convention resolutions versus election platforms, standing laws, and whether an endorsement made before 2027 counts as the starting state.
2. Publish a case table (country, year, actor, text, verdict) so readers can check the base rate.
findings.decision_impact: The owner's goal is that every assumption is falsifiable. As written, the endorsement rows and the base rate cannot be scored unambiguously. Fix before publishing.

findings.claim: The Brazil note calls Law 10.835 'a universal statute' and says the 2023 Bolsa Família law 'calls itself a step toward it'. Yet the engine starts Brazil un-endorsed, and the model gives 0.4% that Brazil endorses by 2028.
findings.evidence:
1. The left-led government of 2023-26 carries a statutory statement (Lei 14.601 Art. 1 §1) and a 2022 platform line backing a universal basic citizenship income.
2. Lula's 2026 platform dropped the idea: 'A ideia proposta pelo petista em 2022, de caminhar para uma renda básica de cidadania, perdeu espaço no documento atual' (Gazeta do Povo, 17 Aug 2026).
3. Under the model's lapse rule (engine.js:276), a Lula win would carry the 2023 endorsement forward, because the government type does not change. In a scratch run with Brazil starting endorsed when the 2027 government is left-led, Brazil's chance of a UBI of any size by 2040 rises from 1.09% to 19.29%, and at 6.7% from 0.52% to 5.50%.
4. The one historical case, 2004, went endorsement, then law, then no payment. The engine cannot represent that: passage always draws an amount of at least 1.11% of GDP per head (engine.js:287).
findings.fix:
1. Decide whether Lei 14.601 §1 is a standing endorsement and set Brazil's starting state to match.
2. State how a re-elected Lula resolves the Brazil 'Checkable soon' row.
3. Acknowledge that Law 10.835 shows passage without funding, and model it as an outcome or explain why it is excluded.
findings.decision_impact: This affects Brazil's numbers and its near-term row. Fix before publishing. It does not affect the US headline.

findings.claim: The Canada note lists only the 2024 C-223 vote and the 2026 convention.
findings.evidence: CBC (10 Apr 2021): the governing Liberal Party's policy convention endorsed a resolution 'calling for the establishment of a universal basic income (UBI)' with 77% support. Its text centres on 'seniors and low-income Canadians'. I did not see the full resolution text, and it did not enter the 2021 election platform.
findings.fix: Add the 2021 resolution to the Canada note and classify it under the clarified rule. Under the model's type definitions it falls in 'other' (a Liberal minority).
findings.decision_impact: Completeness of the record. Polish.

findings.claim: endorseSource marks R_normal and O_normal (PERT 0.001, 0.004, 0.012) as 'data' in all ten countries.
findings.evidence: app.js:353-354 shows the base-rate note only on the L_normal row. No text anywhere derives 0.4% for right-led or other governments, and the pooled calculation behind the claim uses 1% for every type.

reviewed.summary: Most country facts I checked (roughly 60 items across all ten countries) are accurate and correctly sourced: the Thomson et al. figures, the US trifecta list, C-223's 54-273, Burnham's quote and premiership, SPD 'falsch', the Linke 2024 override, Hamburg 62.7/37.3, the 5 March 2026 Grundsicherung vote, Sumar's €550, the Catalan pilot, Lee's positions and the Basic Income Planning Team, the Takaichi/Ishin/Team Mirai claims, Leigh's quote and role, the Australian AI response, and Brazil's laws. One blocker: the claim repeated in every country's endorseBaseNote, the paper (index.qmd:186), app.js:379 and ubi_model.py that no government among the ten endorsed a strict UBI in about 75 terms since 2000. That claim is contradicted under the paper's own endorsement definition. Lula signed Law 10.835/2004, a universal, unconditional, equal-value annual citizen's income, and Lei 14.601/2023 calls Bolsa Família a step toward it; the dashboard itself says 'a universal statute already exists'. Canada's governing Liberals adopted a UBI resolution 491-85 in 2021, and Korea's governing DP ran on a universal payment in 2022. This calibration underpins the 'data'-labelled no-shock endorsement priors and the paper's 'record rules out v1' argument. Fix it by tightening the definition and listing the excluded cases, or by recounting and refitting, which would raise the 11.7% 'any endorsement by 2030' figure. Two majors: Spain's passNote wrongly says Spanish governments are usually minority coalitions (the first coalition was in 2020; Thomson's Spanish cases were single-party high fulfillers), and Australia's passNote says the Senate 'can delay' when it can reject bills and Labor lacks a Senate majority. The rest are minor: C-223 framing (28 Liberals voted yes) and the omitted 2021 convention; France's debt is stale (119.0% at end-Q2 2026, not 115.6%); UK £13bn headroom is an analyst estimate; Hamon's first-round platform was income-tested; Korea's 2027 pilot is a conditional participation income; Japan's April 2027 measure is a bridging payment before the FY2029 credit; the 11% should be 10%; several priors do not follow from their cited anchors (the US passage mode is above the note's 'about half'; the coalition odds imply about 0.37 rather than 0.5; the 6/7 trifecta base rate against a 64% prior; Korea 2028 allows an impossible right-led state; UK vs Korea no-shock prior rule); and small figure inconsistencies. The paper adds that 'the record rules out the no-shock rates the first version implied.' findings.evidence: Read the text of Brazil's Lei 10.835 (8 Jan 2004) on planalto.gov.br. It was signed by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and, from 2005, creates a 'renda básica de cidadania' as the right of all resident Brazilians 'não importando sua condição socioeconômica', paid annually, 'de igual valor para todos', optionally in monthly instalments. That is a head of government signing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment into law. Read Lei 14.601/2023, Art. 1 §1, also signed by Lula: Bolsa Família 'constitui etapa do processo gradual e progressivo de implementação da universalização da renda básica de cidadania'. Your own BRA endorseNote (line 283) says 'A universal statute already exists'. Other governing-party cases that fit the paper's own definition: (a) Canada, April 2021. The governing Liberals' convention passed a caucus-co-sponsored resolution calling on the government to 'develop and implement a universal basic income', 491-85, and it became official party policy (search results citing CBC, Globe and Mail, TNC). (b) South Korea, 2022. The governing DP's presidential candidate Lee pledged a universal payment of 1 million won a year (Korea Herald / BIEN search results; the KOR note itself says so). (c) Germany. The Greens' 2020 Grundsatzprogramm says 'orientieren wir uns an der Leitidee eines Bedingungslosen Grundeinkommens', and the Greens were in government 2021-24. Executed calc.py: with 2 endorsements in 75 terms, P(exactly 2) is 0.133 at a 1% rate and 0.270 at 3%. The record would then favour 3% over 1%, the reverse of the note's argument that 0/75 gives 47% vs 11%. Separately, paper/index.qmd:176 calls endorsement priors 'judgments ... not estimates from data', which contradicts the 'data' labels.
findings.fix: Choose one. (1) Tighten the endorsement definition, for example to a head-of-government or governing-platform commitment to enact and fund a national UBI within the term. Then list Brazil 2004/2023, Canada 2021, Korea 2022 and the German Greens in the ledger as excluded borderline cases, with the reason for each. (2) Count them, refit the no-shock endorsement priors to k>0, and rerun. Either way, reword 'no endorsement ... by any of the ten governments' and the 'rules out' sentence in app.js:379 and index.qmd:186. Consider whether Brazil should start as already endorsed (L), since a universal statute is on the books.
findings.decision_impact: This is the stated calibration behind the 'data'-labelled no-shock endorsement priors and the paper's main argument for why revision 2 is lower. It is contradicted by a fact the same dashboard states (Brazil's universal statute). If the priors were refit, 'any of the ten endorsing by 2030 (11.7%)' and the no-trigger numbers would rise. votes.reasoning:
The core claim holds. The strongest counterexample is Brazil, and I checked it against the primary text. Lula sanctioned Lei 10.835 on 8 Jan 2004 ("eu sanciono"), during his first term, which falls inside the ~75-term window. Art. 1 grants every resident Brazilian, and foreigners resident 5+ years, an annual cash benefit "não importando sua condição socioeconômica". §2 says the benefit is of "igual valor para todos" and §3 allows monthly instalments. That is universal, unconditional and recurring.

The paper defines an endorsement (index.qmd:86) as "a statement by the head of government, or a governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment". A head of government signing such a law into force goes further than that. Lula also signed Lei 14.601 (19 Jun 2023), whose Art. 1 §1 calls Bolsa Família a stage toward "universalização da renda básica de cidadania" under Lei 10.835.

The copy calls the standard "strict UBI" but never defines "strict" anywhere a reader sees it. The only definition is in research/prompts/endorse.md: "universal, unconditional, recurring", and the Brazilian law meets it. The only possible defence is §1: phased rollout at executive discretion, needy first, amount set by the executive. That is a reason to list Brazil as an excluded borderline case, not a reason to say "none".

Nothing handles this elsewhere:
- The paper never mentions the Brazilian statute.
- On Brazil's panel, the ledger shows endorseBaseNote ("None of the ten governments endorsed...", source label "data", L_normal row) directly above endorseNote ("A universal statute already exists"). Readers see the contradiction side by side.
- engine.js:262 starts every country non-endorsed, including Lula's current government, which signed the 2023 law.
- The "~75 terms" list and its case coding are not in the repo (research/out is empty), so readers cannot check the count.

South Korea 2022 is a fair second case under the "governing party's platform" clause. Kyunghyang (11 Feb 2022) reports that Lee's official 10 pledges filed with the National Election Commission included 전국민 기본소득: 250,000 won a year, rising to 1M won within the term. The DP was the governing party at the time. The endorse prompt marks this "(campaign only)", but the public definition does not exclude campaign platforms.

Canada 2021 is confirmed only through a secondary source (TNC). The governing Liberals' caucus-co-sponsored resolution to "develop and implement a universal basic income" passed 491-85 and became official party policy. Its substance may have been income-tested, and a party resolution is not the election platform, so it is borderline. The German Greens' "Leitidee" (2020, junior partner 2021-24) is the weakest of the four.

Where the finding overstates:
- The claim that the record "would then favour 3% over 1%" needs k=2. I reproduced P(k=2) = 0.133 at 1% and 0.270 at 3%.
- With Brazil alone (k=1) the record still favours 1%: 0.357 vs 0.236, a likelihood ratio of 1.5 instead of the 4.6 that k=0 gives. The note's "rules out" rhetoric does not survive even k=1.
- "Would rise" for 11.7% and the no-trigger numbers is directionally right but not rerun (not verified).

Severity: blocker under the rubric. The false sentence appears in all ten ledger rows labelled "data", in both Revisions sections, and in model/ubi_model.py. It is the paper's stated main reason revision 2 is lower, and the dashboard contradicts it visibly.

Secondary points:
- index.qmd:176 and app.js:377 call the endorsement priors "judgments informed by the base rates", while the ledger labels them "data". The two are inconsistent.
- The note's "11%" is 0.97^75 = 10.2%, which rounds to 10% (minor).

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real. The strongest counterexample is Brazil, and I checked it against the primary text.

**Brazil contradicts the claim.** Lei 10.835 (8 Jan 2004), signed by LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA, creates from 2005 a "renda básica de cidadania":
- It is a right of all resident Brazilians "não importando sua condição socioeconômica".
- It is paid annually, "de igual valor para todos" (§2), optionally in monthly instalments (§3).

Lei 14.601 (19 Jun 2023), also signed by Lula, says in Art. 1 §1 that Bolsa Família "constitui etapa do processo gradual e progressivo de implementação da universalização da renda básica de cidadania". The paper defines an endorsement (index.qmd:86) as "a statement by the head of government … backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment". A head of government signing such a statute meets that definition, and it happened twice since 2000.

**The page contradicts itself.** The clean-record sentence says no government in about 75 terms endorsed a strict UBI. It appears in 10 countries.js notes, app.js:379, index.qmd:186 and ubi_model.py:100. In the Brazil ledger it renders as the note on the L_normal row, labelled "data". The next row in the same table shows BRA endorseNote: "A universal statute already exists (Law 10.835/2004…), and the 2023 Bolsa Família law calls itself a step toward it." A careful reader will see both. Brazil's 2004 law is also the best-known national UBI statute in the literature.

**The defence is weak.** One could argue that "strict UBI" excludes Brazil's law, because it phases in with priority to the neediest (§1) and never set an amount. But neither the dashboard nor the paper defines "strict", and the paper's stated definition has no amount or implementation test.

**The other cases are weaker but real.** Search results (CBC, Globe and Mail, Hill Times headlines) confirm that the governing Liberals' April 2021 convention passed a UBI resolution 491-85, reported as becoming official party policy. That is a convention resolution, not a platform, so it could be excluded with a stated reason. I did not verify the Korea 2022 or German Greens cases.

**"Rules out" is false even if the record is 0/75.** Binomial check: P(0 of 75) is 0.471 at a 1% rate and 0.102 at 3%. That is a likelihood ratio of about 4.6, which does not rule anything out. With two events the ratio reverses: P(2) is 0.133 at 1% and 0.270 at 3%. The note's "11%" matches about 72 terms, not 75 (at 75 it is 10.2%), which is minor. There is also a labelling inconsistency: index.qmd:176 calls endorsement priors "judgments … not estimates from data", while the ledger and the Python model label the no-shock priors "data".

**Impact on numbers.** I ran the dashboard engine at N=100k with seed 20260929. The baseline reproduces the committed results.json: US ($6,000 threshold) 2.55% by 2040, at least one of ten 17.84%, any of ten endorsing by 2030 11.73%.

| Scenario | US by 2040 | At least one of ten by 2040 | Any of ten endorsing by 2030 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 2.55% | 17.84% | 11.73% |
| All no-shock endorsement rates ×2 | 2.56% | 21.24% | 19.32% |
| All no-shock endorsement rates ×3 | 2.59% | 24.52% | 26.50% |
| Left no-shock ×3 only | 2.57% | 21.75% | 22.20% |
| Brazil left no-shock set to about 0.5 (proxy for "already endorsed") | 2.55% | 20.51% | 31.15% |

US given no trigger stays below 0.1% in every scenario (0.02% at ×3).

So the US headline is robust. The multi-country headlines ("17.8%", "11.7%") change materially under any refit. The "11.7%" figure is the paper's "sharpest test", and its resolution is ambiguous from day one: Brazil's governing law already states the universalization goal, and the model gives Lula about 45% to win on 4 Oct 2026.

**Why blocker.** As published, the page and paper make a false factual claim, labelled "data", ten times. It is the only stated evidence for the no-shock priors and one of the three stated reasons revision 2 is lower. The page's own Brazil row contradicts it, and it undermines the owner's "everything falsifiable incl. assumptions" goal. The fix is cheap. Tightening the definition and listing exclusions keeps every number unchanged. A refit changes the multi-country numbers but not the US one.

Aside: tripling no-shock endorsement barely moves the US 2040 figure. So "the record rules out the no-shock rates revision 1 implied" is probably not a material driver of the US drop from 9.6% to 2.5%. I did not run a decomposition; not verified.

findings.claim: ESP passNote: 'Spanish governments are usually minority coalitions; coalitions have 72-76% lower odds of fulfilling pledges (Thomson et al. 2017).'
findings.evidence: Spain's January 2020 PSOE-Unidas Podemos cabinet was the first coalition government since the restoration of democracy (search results: Wikipedia 2019-2020 government formation, Al Jazeera, Euronews). Every Spanish government before 2020 was single-party. Thomson et al. votes.reasoning:
The core claim reproduces, so I could not refute it. dashboard/src/countries.js line 378 sets the AUS passNote to "Single-party Westminster majorities fulfil pledges at the highest rates (Thomson et al. 2017); the Senate can delay." At app.js line 357 this note is shown to readers only on the left-led passage row of the assumption ledger, beside Labor's roughly 70% passage prior.

"The Senate can delay" misstates how the Australian Senate works. Section 53 of the Constitution says "Except as provided in this section, the Senate shall have equal power with the House of Representatives in respect of all proposed laws." The Senate cannot originate or amend money bills, but it can reject any bill, including supply, as it did in 1975. A deadlock ends only through the section 57 route: the Senate fails to pass the bill again after three months, the whole parliament goes to a double-dissolution election, and the bill then passes a joint sitting. "Can delay" describes the UK House of Lords or the Irish Seanad, not an elected chamber with equal powers. It also hides the real constraint: Labor holds 30 of 76 Senate seats (Wikipedia composition table; the change came when Tyrrell joined Labor on 14 May 2026). The paper (index.qmd) does not repeat the Senate claim, so only the dashboard note is affected.

The Thomson part of the finding also holds, though it is weaker. Australia is not among Thomson's 12 countries: the list is at line 196 of research/thomson2017.txt and Table 1 is at line 1731. The note does not claim Australia is in the sample, so this is an extrapolation, not a false statement. Two caveats go beyond the finding:
- Every single-party-majority case in Thomson's sample (UK, Canada, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Bulgaria, US) lacks an elected upper house with full veto power.
- Thomson's own result is "single-party executives, both with and without legislative majorities" (line 1048). In Model 1 of Table 2, single-party minority governments have an odds ratio of 1.46 against the single-party-majority reference (p=.04). "Single-party majorities fulfil pledges at the highest rates" is therefore slightly overstated as a regression claim. Descriptively, the UK single-party majorities had the highest rate (86%).

Severity: this is a wrong mechanism claim that a reader sees, and it supports the prior of the highest-forecast country (4.6% by 2040 in paper/_includes/table_countries.md). It changes no number, which makes it major, not blocker.

Parts of the finding's proposed fix are wrong:
- The arithmetic. Labor 30 plus Greens 10 is 40, which clears the 39 needed out of 76. The Senate President, Labor's Sue Lines, keeps a deliberative vote. So at the current composition Labor needs only the Greens, not "the Greens plus at least one more senator." Since the Greens back "an unconditional livable income", a high left-led passage prior stays defensible. The note should say why, not claim that the Senate can only delay.
- "Consider a lower R prior because the Coalition is a coalition." This is a judgment call, not a defect. The Liberal-National Coalition is a standing pre-election coalition, and Thomson's pre-election-coalition coefficient (odds ratio 2.92 in Model 1) pushes the other way. The right-led passage row shows no passNote, so no false text backs that prior.

The finding is real. The Australia passNote (dashboard/src/countries.js:378) says "the Senate can delay", but the Senate can reject any bill. Section 53 stops the Senate from originating money bills and from amending tax or ordinary-annual-services appropriation bills. It then says: "Except as provided in this section, the Senate shall have equal power with the House of Representatives in respect of all proposed laws." Section 57 settles a Senate that "rejects or fails to pass" a bill only through a double dissolution, a fresh election and then a joint sitting. That is a veto, not a delay. The same edition's overview adds: "Often the Government does not have a majority of seats in the Senate." Wikipedia's Australian Senate article says governments have held a Senate majority only after the 1975, 1977 and 2004 elections. The project's own research file contradicts the note too: research/country_research.json (AUS system_notes) says a nationwide cash benefit "needs a House majority ... plus a Senate majority."

Where the claim appears: app.js:357 renders passNote only on Australia's "left-led government ... becomes law within the term" row of the assumption ledger. It is the only justification shown for Australia's 70% left-led passage prior, which the paper's table_inputs repeats. Australia is the country with the highest forecast (4.6% by 2040). The note puts Australia's Senate in the same class as the weak UK and Canadian upper houses, where both get the same 70%. For a careful reader that is a false account of how Australian bills pass, and Max's no-fabricated-mechanisms rule makes this kind of error the one to fix before publishing.

Why major and not blocker: the note is text. No published number changes. I re-ran the engine with 200,000 histories and seed 20260929, and the baseline reproduced the published figures exactly: AUS 4.61% by 2040 and 12.88% by 2050, any of the ten 17.80%, US 2.49%. The corrected fact partly supports the current prior. Labor holds 30 of 76 Senate seats and the Greens 10, so Labor plus Greens is 40, above the 39 needed. The Greens back "an unconditional livable income", so a Labor government that endorsed a UBI would have a Senate partner ready. A 70% prior for left-led governments stays defensible once the note is corrected. For scale, if the owner lowered the left-led passage prior to 0.3/0.5/0.7, Australia would fall from 4.6% to 3.7% by 2040, tying Canada for first. Any of the ten would fall from 17.8% to 17.2%, and the US would stay at 2.5%. Lowering the right-led prior as well gives Australia 3.4% and any of the ten 17.1%. reviewed.summary:
Don't publish revision 2 as-is: the page and paper make a false claim about the unemployment trigger, the model's central testable event. They say its second condition (real GDP at or above its previous peak) separates an AI-driven labor shock from an ordinary recession, because GDP was below its peak in all eleven historical +3-point unemployment episodes. That is true only in each episode's first month, which is the only month the repo's script checks. In 7 of the 11 episodes, GDP got back to its peak while unemployment was still 3 or more points up. Applied literally with the pre-recession year as the baseline, the trigger would have fired after 4 of the last 5 US recessions (1975, 1983, 2010-13, 2021). A tested fix exists. If the rule requires that GDP never fell below its peak during the unemployment rise, it fires zero times in history across the nine countries with data. Alternatively, keep the rule, drop the 'separates… / without a recession' wording, and add non-AI recessions to the timing prior.

Major findings:
- **Episode count.** The trigger script silently drops episodes that start before its GDP data (Canada 1958, Spain 1993), and Brazil's history was never checked. So 'eleven episodes in all ten countries' is wrong.
- **Prior vs resolution.** The timing priors were set for an economist-attributed AI shock but resolve on raw unemployment and GDP data with no attribution.
- **Endorsement record.** The 'no endorsement in about 75 terms' base rate, badged as data, is contested by the page's own Brazil fact (Law 10.835/2004, a universal cash-benefit statute). It is also contested by South Korea's People Power Party platform, which backed basic income while that party governed in 2022-25. The ~75 terms are listed nowhere in the repo. Doubling the no-shock endorsement rates moves 'any of the ten endorses by 2030' from 11.7% to 19.4% and the all-ten 2040 figure from 17.8% to 21.2%.
- **Korea.** It could already be scored as endorsed from its May 2026 plan naming basic income as an AI-era safety net. Treating it that way moves the all-ten 2040 figure from 17.8% to 22.5%.
- **Endorsement definition.** It differs between the dashboard and the paper ('the governing party' vs 'a governing party'), so junior partners such as Japan's Ishin and Spain's Sumar may or may not count.
- **Overclaim.** The dashboard says every assumption can turn out wrong, but gives no scoring rule, and 44% of simulated histories never test the shock-conditional inputs. A sharp test is available: two or more of the ten endorsing by 2030 with no trigger has a 0.3% chance under the model.
- **Ratchet row.** It shows 13%, but the observable chance of a raise in a given year is 5.6%.
- **Other countries' triggers.** Their rows say they resolve 'when the US trigger is met', despite lags of up to 3-7 years. The ledger also doesn't state that no country can meet its trigger unless the US does.

Positive evidence: the trigger data and pipeline reproduce exactly and are current (US October 2025 is correctly missing because of the shutdown). The trigger levels are right, and every market anchor exists with the stated price and trader count. The 'Checkable soon' table and the headline numbers (US 2.5%, any of the ten 17.8%) reproduce exactly. Tests pass (82 vitest, 7 pytest), and nothing near-term has clearly resolved yet. All findings except the blocker are fixable without touching the headline US number. Scratch scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Applications/da707ee8-bdb9-43d0-bb83-c08c894e427d/scratchpad/wf-review/falsifiability/ (trigger/per_episode.py, conj.py, episodes_all.py, alt_def.py; dash/soon.mjs, rc.mjs, rule.mjs, normal2x.mjs, ledger.mjs; ledger.txt).

Trigger levels in countries.js (USA 7.3, GBR 7.9, CAN 9.9, DEU 6.7, FRA 10.7, ESP 13.5, JPN 5.5, KOR 5.8, AUS 7.2, BRA 8.9) equal round(2025 average + 3, 1) from the committed CSVs. The paper's table_trigger.md matches.

2025 data are complete: 12 monthly values for every country except the US, which has 11 because October 2025 is blank. The blank appears in the repo CSV and on live FRED (curl of fredgraph.csv). Live FRED UNRATE and LRHUTTTTGBM156S values for 2025-26 match the repo CSVs, and the GBR 2025 average recomputes to 4.85. Brazil uses SIDRA variable 4099 rolling quarters, with 12 values for 2025.

The series named in each ledger trigger row is the series the script uses (countries.js trigger.source matches the script's C mapping, including IBGE 6381 for Brazil). The latest values and GDP-at-peak status in the notes match triggers.json, including France being below its peak.

The 2028 prior (4%/8%/15%, mean 8.5%) is correctly badged 'judgment'.

The paper honestly says conditional inputs resolve only when their condition occurs (index.qmd:166).

Korea: search results describe UBI reframed as 'basic society', with the ambiguity noted in the Korea finding. Brazil's 4 Oct election and the US 3 Nov midterms are still open and resolve within weeks.

findings.claim: The page says that in all eleven historical +3-point episodes real GDP was below its previous peak, 'so the second condition separates a labor-displacing technology shock from an ordinary recession'. The same claim appears in paper/index.qmd:74 ('In all eleven, real GDP was below its previous peak'), in the abstract (index.qmd:8, 'without a recession'), in the intro (index.qmd:34, 'while the economy keeps growing') and in the fig_model label (paper/scripts/build_assets.py:241, 'without a recession').
findings.evidence: compute_triggers.py tests GDP only in an episode's first month (lines 44-52). I checked every month of every episode instead (scratch trigger/per_episode.py). In 7 of the 11 episodes, the 12-month unemployment average was still 3 or more points above its level 24 months earlier while real GDP was at or above its previous peak: USA 1975-10..1976-06 (9 months), USA 2010-10..2010-12, USA 2021-01..2021-06, CAN 1983-10..1984-05, KOR 1999-04..2000-02, AUS 1983-10..1984-08 and AUS 1992-04..1993-04. The count is still 7 of 11 when a quarter's GDP counts only from 4 months after its start, which allows for publication lag. I also applied the literal trigger (a fixed calendar-year baseline plus 3, with GDP at or above its peak) using the year before each US recession as the baseline (conj.py, variant B). It is met in 1975-10 (1973 baseline), 1983-04 (1979), 2010-10 through 2013-08 (2007) and 2021-01 (2019): 4 of the last 5 US recessions, all ordinary ones. It also fires in recoveries in GBR (1993-94), CAN, DEU (1996-99, 2005-06), ESP, KOR and AUS. A fix I tested (alt_def.py) requires that real GDP never fell below its running peak since the baseline (or during the 24-month rise). Under that rule there are 0 historical hits in all nine countries with data.
findings.fix: Choose one of two routes. (a) Redefine the GDP condition as 'real GDP has not been below its previous peak in any quarter since the rise began'. This had zero historical false positives. Anchor the window to the start of the rise, because France's GDP is below its peak in 2026Q2. (b) Keep the definition, delete the 'separates… from an ordinary recession' and 'without a recession' wording everywhere, and add a non-AI recession-recovery route to the trigger-timing prior. Either way, re-run the historical check on every month, not only the first month of each episode.
findings.decision_impact: Publishing as-is states a false historical claim about the model's central falsifiable event. A severe ordinary recession followed by a recovery could resolve the 'Trigger met by 2028/2030' predictions YES. The paper (index.qmd:164) would then tell readers that the AI-market anchors were too pessimistic, which is a wrong inference. The headline numbers are unchanged by a wording fix; a definition change would need the prior re-examined. Fix before publishing.

votes.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding; it reproduces. research/trigger/compute_triggers.py (lines 44-52) checks GDP only in the first month of each episode (`if hit and not in_ep: cur = gdp_at(d)`). So "real GDP was below its previous peak" is true only at each episode's first month.

The trigger the page and paper define is a monthly conjunction with no requirement that GDP never fell. The ledger (app.js:335) reads "12-month average at or above X% while real GDP is at or above its previous peak", resolved "Monthly". Under that definition, ordinary recession recoveries meet it:

- **Every month of every episode:** in 7 of the 11 episodes the unemployment condition still held after GDP had regained its prior peak. The cases are USA 1975-10..1976-06, USA 2010-10..12, USA 2021-01..06, CAN 1983-10..1984-05, KOR 1999-04..2000-02, AUS 1983-10..1984-08 and AUS 1992-04..1993-04.
- **Publication lag:** with a 4-month lag on GDP it is still 7 of 11.
- **Literal fixed baseline, US:** the conjunction is met after the 1973-75, 1981-82, 2007-09 and 2020 recessions. Every US recession since 1948 that pushed the 12-month average 3 points above the prior year's level met it in recovery. The 1957, 1969, 1990 and 2001 recessions never reached the unemployment level at all.
- **A 2020-sized shock from today's baseline:** the 7.3% level plus GDP at its peak would still hold in 2021-05.

So "the second condition separates a labor-displacing technology shock from an ordinary recession" (app.js:373, paper/index.qmd:74) is false by the repo's own data. "In all eleven, real GDP was below its previous peak" is true only at the first month and misleading in context. I confirmed that both sentences appear in the staged maxghenis.com PR #62 pages (public/ubi-forecast/index.html and paper/web/index.html).

This matters for falsifiability as well as wording. The "Checkable soon" trigger predictions (US 8.5% by 2028, 18.4% by 2030) resolve from official series (app.js:313). But the prior in countries.js GLOBALS is described as "economist-attributed AI displacement" and is anchored only to AI markets. An ordinary severe recession followed by a recovery could therefore resolve them YES. Paper line 164 would then draw the wrong inference ("the AI-market anchors were too pessimistic").

The headline numbers do not change: the engine draws trigger timing from the GLOBALS prior, not from the data. But the rubric counts a false or materially misleading statement to readers as a blocker, and this one concerns the model's central falsifiable event, in the abstract, introduction, model section and dashboard.

Small corrections to the finding:
- "4 of the last 5 US recessions" is imprecise. The hits are the 1973-75, 1981-82, 2007-09 and 2020 recessions, not the last five, though no US recession that met the unemployment condition failed the conjunction.
- The finding missed that "eleven" itself undercounts. The unemployment records hold 13 episodes, and the two without GDP data are dropped: CAN 1958-59 and ESP 1993-95. So the paper's "Canada three times ... Spain ... once" and the countries.js notes ("Since 1955, 3 rises" for CAN, "Since 1986, 1 rise" for ESP) are also wrong.

The proposed fix (a) holds up: requiring that no quarter from 2 months before the rise window through the current month is below the running peak gives 0 historical hits across all nine countries with data.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real. Both the dashboard and the paper say the GDP condition separates a technology shock from an ordinary recession. That is false for the trigger as the model defines it: a 12-month unemployment average at least 3 points above a fixed baseline while real GDP is at or above its previous peak. Unemployment stays high after output has recovered, so the condition is met during the recovery from an ordinary recession.

What I found:
(1) compute_triggers.py (lines 44-52) checks GDP only in the first month of each episode, and every first month falls in the downturn. That is why triggers.json shows "jobless_growth": false for all 11 episodes. When I checked every month instead, 7 of the 11 episodes have months where the unemployment rise still held and GDP was at or above its peak. The months match the reviewer's list exactly: USA 1975-10..1976-06, 2010-10..12, 2021-01..06; CAN 1983-10..1984-05; KOR 1999-04..2000-02; AUS 1983-10..1984-08 and 1992-04..1993-04. The count stays 7 of 11 when each quarter's GDP counts only from 4 months after the quarter starts, to allow for publication lag.
(2) I replayed the literal US trigger, using the year before each recession as the baseline. It fires in 1975-10 (1973 baseline), 1983-04 (1979), 2010-10 through 2013-08 (2007) and 2021-01 (2019). It does not fire for 1989 or 2000. At the model's actual 7.3% threshold, history would meet the trigger in 1975-77, 1981, 1983-85, 1992-93, 2010-13 and 2021.
(3) Across 69 overlapping US baseline years, the literal trigger fires within five years of the baseline (the analogue of the 2025 baseline and a 2030 deadline) for 10-16% of them. The range depends on publication lag, and the overlapping windows make this a crude estimate. The model publishes 18.4% for "US trigger met by 2030" and 8.5% by 2028. Its priors in countries.js lines 14-27 are anchored only to AI markets and have no route for an ordinary recession. So the event the paper offers as its first falsification test (index.qmd:164, "if the trigger arrives much earlier, the AI-market anchors were too pessimistic") could resolve YES through an ordinary recession. That route is comparable in size to the whole AI prior, and the paper would then draw the wrong conclusion.

Why blocker: the trigger is the model's central event. The abstract says "nearly all of that probability runs through the unemployment trigger." The page and paper tell readers, in five places, that this event excludes ordinary recessions, and it does not. That meets the rubric's "false or materially misleading" test even though a wording fix leaves the headline outputs unchanged. Those outputs come from the AI-anchored prior, not from the history. If the owner keeps the definition and honestly adds a recession route to the prior, the trigger prior and every headline would rise.

The per-country notes in countries.js lines 129 and 232 undercount the same way (Canada 3, which should be 4; Spain 1, which should be 2).

I could not refute the finding. Every part of it reproduces except one supporting count, which is overstated.

1. **The prior's definition.** countries.js:10-12 and model/ubi_model.py:55-56 both define the timing priors as the onset of a "sustained, economist-attributed AI displacement" of about 3 pp. The GLOBAL_NOTES, which the ledger's Basis column shows to readers, anchor each year to markets on AI-attributed or AGI-driven unemployment.

2. **The anchor market.** The Manifold API shows the anchor market at 23% with 175 bettors. Its description says it "only resolves Yes if AI ... is directly responsible for at least 3 percentage points".

3. **The resolution.** app.js:321-330 relabels the same priors as "The US trigger is met by the end of 20XX". It resolves them "from BLS unemployment (FRED UNRATE) and BEA real GDP (FRED GDPC1)", with no attribution test. The paper (index.qmd:74-76) does the same: it defines the event statistically and calls the prior "anchored to markets on AGI and AI-driven unemployment".

4. **The displayed values.** pertMean is (lo+4·mode+hi)/6 (engine.js:119). It gives 8.5%, 18.3%, 33.3%, 43.3% and 55%, matching the finding.

5. **Whether the copy already handles it.** The copy's defence is that the GDP-at-peak condition "separates a labor-displacing technology shock from an ordinary recession". It rests on compute_triggers.py, which checks GDP only in the first month of each episode. The forward trigger as written has no such restriction: any month where the 12-month average is at or above the level and GDP is at or above its previous peak meets it.

   I applied that literal rule to the repo's own UNRATE and GDPC1 data, using a pre-recession calendar-year average as the baseline. Ordinary recessions meet it during their recoveries:
   - 1983-04: 12-month average 10.17, GDP 1.02% above its prior peak.
   - 2010-10: 9.67, GDP 0.1% above.
   - 2021-01: 8.33 against a 6.7 level from the 2019 baseline, GDP 0.58% above.
   - 1975-10: met with a 1973 baseline, not with a 1972 baseline.

   The event that resolves the row therefore includes non-AI outcomes that the AI-anchored prior does not price. The mismatch is visible to readers, not only in a code comment.

6. **The overstated count.** "4 of the last 5 US recessions" is too high. 1990-91 and 2001 cannot meet any trigger of +3 points: their 12-month averages peaked at 7.49 against a level of 8.3, and at about 6 against a level of 7.0. The accurate statement is 3 of the last 5 (1981-82, 2007-09, 2020). Put another way, 3 or 4 of the 4 US episodes with a rise of 3 points or more met it, depending on the 1970s baseline year. This does not weaken the finding.

**Severity.** Major, not blocker. The mismatch does not change any computed headline number, but it makes the "falsifiable" ledger row misleading about the event its number prices. The finding itself notes that the same fix resolves the related blocker.

**The proposed fix works.** I tested a stricter definition over all US history since 1948: the 12-month average rises at least 3 points above its value 24 months earlier, and GDP was not below its previous peak in any of the preceding 8 quarters. It never fires. Under that definition the AI-market anchors become a reasonable proxy.

I could not refute this finding. The dashboard and the paper define an endorsement differently, and both staged pages carry the two versions.

**The two definitions**
- Dashboard (app.js:313, and the staged public/ubi-forecast/index.html on the ubi-revision-2 branch of maxghenis.com): "the governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a qualifying UBI".
- Paper (index.qmd:86, and the staged paper/web/index.html): "a governing party's platform or coalition agreement, backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment".

They differ in two ways:
1. "The governing party" (the lead party) against "a governing party" (which takes in junior partners).
2. "Qualifying UBI" against a definition with no amount. On the dashboard, "qualifying" points to an amount floor: engine.js:287 says a qualifying program is at least about 1.1% of GDP per head, and app.js:157 calls it "the smallest program that qualifies". The paper mixes the two in one paragraph: its previous sentence also says "a qualifying UBI".

**Both example cases reproduce from primary sources**
- Ishin's 2026 platform (o-ishin.jp/policy/8saku2026.html) promises a minimum income "給付付き税額控除、負の所得税またはベーシックインカム". The "または" (or) makes basic income one of three alternatives. The repo's own research file says Ishin joined the cabinet on 17 Sep 2026. I took that from the file and did not check it externally.
- Movimiento Sumar presented a €550-a-month youth basic income for ages 18-21 at its party conference. It is described as "de carácter universal" and as a "punto de partida" (starting point) toward a guaranteed income for the whole population. Sumar is a junior partner in the PSOE–Sumar government (countries.js:244).

- The paper calls the endorsement forecast "the sharpest test: 11.7%" (index.qmd:164; `all_end2030` = 11.7% in _variables.yml).

- The calibration line "no endorsement of a strict UBI … in about 75 terms" (app.js:379, countries.js endorseBaseNote) uses a third undefined phrase, "strict UBI". So the base rate and the forecast may not be measured on the same definition.

**Nothing else covers it.** The ledger rows (app.js:353), the template sliders, and the paper's table caption (index.qmd:162) add no tighter definition.

votes.reasoning:
I tried to refute both parts of the finding, and both hold.

1. The resolution text is wrong. In dashboard/src/app.js line 338 the ledger row reads "If the US trigger is met, X's is met too", and its Resolves column says "When the US trigger is met". The engine (engine.js lines 233-239) sets `met = exposed && Number.isFinite(on) ? on + lag : Infinity`. The lag is a PERT draw from countries.js, and its high end is 2 years for CAN, 3 for GBR, KOR and AUS, 5 for DEU, FRA, ESP and JPN, and 7 for BRA. When the US trigger is met, the other country's trigger usually has not been met yet. The lag's low end is -0.5 for GBR, CAN and AUS and -1 for KOR, so a "yes" can also come before the US date. No deadline is given for a "no". The next row ("...and within this many years of the US", which resolves "When both triggers are met") states the window, so a careful reader could piece the rule together. But the row's own resolution is still wrong, and a "no" never becomes checkable. That cuts directly against the owner's goal that every assumption be falsifiable.

2. A structural assumption is missing from the ledger. The same line of the engine means no country can ever meet its trigger in a history where the US trigger is not met by 2050. I reran the engine at the default seed with n=200,000: 88,778 histories had no US trigger, and non-US triggers in those histories numbered 0. That matches the other reviewer's count exactly. I found partial disclosure only:
- paper/index.qmd line 78 says each country's trigger has "a probability conditional on the US trigger".
- Line 132 says the countries "share one trigger timing".
- The paper's trigger table headers read "Meets it if the US does" and "Lag behind the US".
- The dashboard's exposure control offers "own chance and lag", "every country", or "US only", with no independent option.

None of these says that a trigger outside the US without a US trigger has probability zero. No ledger row states it, and neither the dashboard's "What it leaves out" nor the paper's limitations paragraph (line 176) mentions it. So a euro-area-only or Korea-only shock would falsify an assumption that is nowhere written down as one.

Two small corrections to the finding itself:
- Lags can also be negative (down to -1 for Korea), so countries can meet their trigger up to 1 calendar year before the US. In 6,955 of the 111,222 histories with a US trigger, some country met its trigger in an earlier calendar year than the US; the per-country gaps ran from -1 to 7 years. Even then, it only happens when the US meets its trigger later.
- The ledger shows the mean exposure (GBR 76.7%). The model only counts triggers met by 2050, which gives an effective P(GBR met by 2050 | US met by 2050) of 74.9%.

Severity: no headline number changes, and nothing published is false outright. But the Resolves text is incorrect, and a zero-probability structural assumption is left out of the one place meant to list every assumption. Given the owner's explicit falsifiability goal, this should be fixed before publishing, so major fits. It sits at the low end of major because the fix is copy only.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and I rate it major.

1. Mechanism (read in engine.js lines 233-239). Each non-US country draws `exposed` (a coin at the exposure mean) and a lag. Then `met = exposed && Number.isFinite(on) ? on + lag : Infinity`, where `on` is the US onset. A non-US trigger therefore exists only in histories where the US trigger is met by 2050. I ran it at n=200,000 with the default seed: 0 non-US triggers across the 88,778 histories with no US trigger. That matches the other reviewer's figure exactly.

2. Resolution text. The ledger row at app.js line 338 says "If the US trigger is met, X's is met too", resolving "When the US trigger is met". That is imprecise. The event resolves at on + lag, and the lags range from a negative lower bound up to a positive upper bound:
   - GBR -0.5 to 3, CAN -0.5 to 2, KOR -1 to 3, AUS -0.5 to 3
   - DEU, FRA, ESP and JPN 0 to 5
   - BRA 0 to 7

   So the row can resolve up to a year before the US trigger or up to 7 years after it. The original finding missed the negative lags.

   Because the event is dated at on + lag, P(met by 2050 | US met by 2050) comes out below the stated exposure. Examples: GBR 0.749 vs 0.767 stated; BRA 0.333 vs 0.358.

   The adjacent row ("...and within this many years of the US") does give the lag range. A careful reader can piece the window together, so the resolution wording alone would be minor.

3. The undisclosed assumption is what makes this major. No row in the ledger, and no line in the paper's Limitations (index.qmd line 176), says that a country cannot meet its trigger unless the US does. Several places suggest the opposite:
   - Paper line 78 says each country "meets its own trigger, defined the same way on its own unemployment and GDP series". It then qualifies this only as "a probability conditional on the US trigger", which never states the complement (zero).
   - The dashboard control reads "Each country's own chance and lag".
   - The KOR note says Korea already reports AI-driven cuts to youth hiring, which points to Korea possibly leading. Yet the model gives Korea's trigger zero chance unless the US trigger also comes.

   The owner's stated goal is "everything falsifiable incl assumptions". A structural zero that a shock starting in Korea or the eurozone would falsify, and that appears in no ledger row, is exactly the kind of gap that goal rules out.

   You can see it in published numbers. In the paper's table_soon.md, "At least one of the ten" meets its trigger by 2030 at 18.5%, against 18.4% for the US alone. My run gives 0.17% for "some country by 2030 but not the US". A careful reader cannot explain why ten countries add almost nothing, because the reason is never stated.

   The multi-country headlines also rest on it: at least one of the ten by 2040 (17.8%), and any government endorsing by 2030 (11.7%). Per table_signposts_all.md, when the US trigger has not been met by 2040, the at-least-one forecast is 4.3%, and that comes only from endorsements in normal times.

4. Why not blocker:
   - Nothing stated is literally false; the assumption is left out, not misstated.
   - The multi-country numbers are computed correctly under the model as coded.
   - The US headlines do not depend on other countries' triggers: 2.5% by 2040, 7.4% by 2050, <0.1% with no trigger, 2.6% endorsement by 2030. The only link between countries is the diffusion risk, which is off by default (DEFAULT_CONTROLS risks all false). The engine test "'the US only' exposure leaves the US forecast unchanged" covers this.

5. A related minor defect I found. Negative lags are not clamped to the present. The code clamps US onset to at least 2026.75, but it does not clamp the non-US date `met`. As a result, some histories date a country's trigger before October 2026:

   | Country | Histories (of 200k) | Share |
   |---|---|---|
   | KOR | 281 | 0.14% |
   | CAN | 109 | |
   | AUS | 37 | |
   | GBR | 29 | |

   This contradicts the data: research/trigger/triggers.json shows Korea's 12-month average at 2.83 against a trigger level of 5.8. The effect on the numbers is tiny.

   The engine test "the trigger never comes before October 2026" checks only the US column. Relatedly, the model's negative lags mean a country can lead the US only in histories where the US follows later, which is a look-ahead the ledger does not disclose either.
