Trigger facts. triggers.json gives the US 2025 average as 4.26% (11 months) and a level of 7.3%. The US episodes 1975-09, 2009-06 and 2020-09, and 11 episodes in total, all with GDP below its prior peak, match the prose for the nine countries with history.

Research tallies. country_research.json verification checks total 332: 264 CONFIRMED, 42 CORRECTED, 7 WRONG, 19 UNVERIFIABLE. fact_link_check.json has 37 facts: 16 SUPPORTED, 21 PARTLY. Both match the paper.

Market claims against markets.json and the live Manifold API (fetched 2026-09-30). The nine third-party markets and their prices and trader counts match. At least 8 open US-UBI markets by others exist (vicli x2, YakshBirla, ahalekelly, NoAnswer, dog, mirrorbot, JaundicedBaboon). The most active has 37 traders. The minimum price/model ratio is 8.9x, supporting 'eight or more times'. The maximum is 50 traders. The two Marshall Islands YES resolutions (2025-11-28 and 2025-12-03) are documented in the research. The 23%, 53% and 72% market anchors appear in countries.js GLOBAL_NOTES and model/README.md.

Citation keys. All 29 cited keys resolve in references.bib. The 18 AI and forecasting references carry verifier checks: 17 CONFIRMED, 1 CORRECTED. The Servan-Schreiber '208 NFL games' and Acemoglu '<1% TFP over ten years' (0.66%) claims match the recorded check evidence.

Repo state. git status shows no tracked or untracked changes (HEAD 2b027ba). Only pre-existing ignored caches were touched: model/.hypothesis from the Hypothesis run. Pytest ran with -p no:cacheprovider and Python with dont_write_bytecode. The scratch HTTP server I started (pid 7685) was stopped.

findings.claim: "In the official records of all ten countries, eleven episodes saw the 12-month unemployment rate rise three points or more above its level two years earlier ... In all eleven, real GDP was below its previous peak." (The same claim appears in the dashboard's How-it-works text, dashboard/src/app.js around line 373: "all eleven episodes on record across the ten countries".)
findings.evidence: research/trigger/triggers.json (read this session): BRA u_start = "2024-09" with episodes [], and countries.js BRA trigger note says "History not checked (series fetched from 2024)." compute_triggers.py needs 11 + 24 months of data before it can flag an episode, so Brazil was never tested. The other series start at USA 1948, CAN/JPN 1955, AUS 1978, GBR/FRA 1983, ESP 1986, KOR 1990 and DEU 1991, which is not the full 'official record'. The count itself is correct for the nine countries checked: USA 1975-09, 2009-06, 2020-09; CAN 3; AUS 2; GBR, ESP, KOR 1 each; total 11, every one with gdp_vs_prior_peak_pct < 0.
findings.fix: Say 'in the OECD harmonised (and BLS) series for nine of the ten countries, back to each series' start (1948-1991); Brazil's series was only checked from 2024'. Or extend compute_triggers.py to a long Brazilian series (e.g., PNAD/PME) before making the claim. Fix the dashboard copy the same way.
findings.decision_impact: This is the empirical basis for the paper's key design choice: the 'jobless growth' condition separates an AI shock from a recession. As written it overclaims coverage. It is quick to fix and does not change any number, but it should be fixed before publishing.

findings.claim: Revisions: "This version splits enactment into the two observable steps above and calibrates the no-shock endorsement rate to the record ... Both changes lower the forecast: endorsing first and passing later takes time, an endorsement lapses when the government changes, and the record rules out the no-shock rates the first version implied." (The dashboard's Revisions paragraph in app.js renderHow says the same.)
findings.evidence: I verified revision 1's figure by running engine.js and countries.js from commit 4c50637 (git show, in scratch): US 2040 = 0.096235 (9.6%), all ten = 0.35647. The live maxghenis.com/ubi-forecast/ also shows 9.6%. I then ran scratch/cf.mjs on the revision 2 US configuration (seed 20260929, n=200k) with no-shock endorsement set so that endorse x pass reproduces revision 1's no-shock enactment rates (L 1-3-7%, R 0.5-2-5%, O 0-0.3-1% per term, divided by pass means of 0.55 and 0.105). Result: 0.026035 against 0.02491. In cf2.mjs, setting every no-shock endorsement to zero gives 0.025155, which is slightly higher than the default. The no-shock calibration therefore explains about 0.1 of the 7.1-point drop, and its sign is not even monotone. The drop comes from the two-step structure and the shock-path numbers. The shock-timing priors (GLOBALS) and US amounts are identical in both revisions.
findings.fix: Attribute the drop to the two-step endorsement-then-passage structure, with its delay and lapse. Add that restoring revision 1's no-shock rates moves the US 2040 figure only from 2.5% to 2.6%, so the base-rate calibration mainly matters for any-size and near-term endorsement questions. Put that counterfactual in results.mjs so the number is generated rather than typed.
findings.decision_impact: This is a mechanism claim that a run contradicts, the kind the owner's 'no fabricated mechanisms' rule targets. The headline is unaffected, but the explanation readers get for the 9.6% to 2.5% revision is wrong in emphasis. It should be fixed before publishing.

findings.claim: "calibrates the no-shock endorsement rate to the record, which has no endorsement of a strict UBI by any of the ten governments in about 75 terms since 2000" (the same claim sits in every countries.js endorseBaseNote and in model/ubi_model.py e_*_normal notes marked DATA).
findings.evidence: The endorse research prompt (research/prompts/endorse.md) asked for 'N governing-party endorsements across M government-terms since 2000', but research/out/ is empty (ls shows 0 files). I found no committed source for 'about 75' or for the zero count. The repo's own Brazil research (research/country_research.json lines 2857 and 3480, URL lei-10835-8-janeiro-2004) says Law 10.835/2004 'creates a universal Renda Básica de Cidadania for Brazilians and foreigners resident 5+ years, regardless of socioeconomic condition'. It also notes that national laws are sanctioned by the president. That is a head-of-government act backing a universal, unconditional, recurring payment inside the 2000+ window, which the paper's endorsement definition (line 86) would appear to count. Separately, the dashboard note's arithmetic is off: 0.99^75 = 0.471 (the note's 47% is correct), but 0.97^75 = 0.102, while the note says 11%.
findings.fix: Commit the endorsement-record research output (the list of terms and candidate endorsements) and cite it. Either count Brazil 2004 (and say why the 2023 Bolsa Familia 'step toward RBC' framing does or does not count) or state the exclusion rule that removes it. Correct 11% to 10%.
findings.decision_impact: This fact is the only 'data' badge on the no-shock endorsement priors, and the paper's 'falsifiable' framing rests on inputs like it. My counterfactual in revision-attribution-noshock shows the US headline barely depends on it, so this is a sourcing and accuracy fix rather than a number change. It should be fixed before publishing.

findings.claim: "Who wins the 2028 election matters far less: a Democratic trifecta gives 2.7% against 2.4% otherwise, because without a shock even a trifecta rarely endorses."
findings.evidence: scratch/cond.mjs (seed 20260929, n=200k): P(US $6k by 2040 | Dem trifecta 2028 and trigger by 2030) = 10.8% (n=11,677), against 8.8% (n=25,042) without a Dem trifecta. findings.claim: "...which is conservation of expected evidence, and the tests check it for every signpost." Line 172: "Each country and each history has its own random stream, so a change to one country's inputs leaves the others' results unchanged."
findings.evidence: dashboard/test/engine.test.js line 38 checks the law of total probability for a single signpost mask (onset < 2031) on synthetic countries, not for every signpost. The identity does hold by construction: I computed max |pS*pIfYes + (1-pS)*pIfNo - pU| = 2.8e-17 over every signpost in results.json. The common-random-numbers test (lines 111-118) runs with risks {}. With the diffusion risk on, one country's enactment changes every other country's endorsement hazard (engine.js line 280), so the unqualified line-172 claim is false in that mode.
findings.fix: Say 'the identity holds by construction and a property test checks it' and add 'except under the policy-diffusion switch' to the random-stream sentence. Optionally, loop the property test over all signpostDefs.
findings.decision_impact: This is wording about validation. No numbers are affected.

findings.claim: The fig_signposts_us.png title reads 'United States, UBI by 2040. Filled: if yes. Hollow: if no. Line: today's forecast.'

findings.claim: Minor accuracy and labeling points in the prose and tables, listed below.

The model discounts the market anchors (shock_by_2030 mean 18%, against the 23% market for unemployment above 10%), so an early trigger would mean the discount was too heavy, not that the markets were too pessimistic. (b) Line 146: 'the proposals of its president's government have been worth about 2% of GDP per head'. countries.js KOR amountNote puts 1.9% on Lee's 2022 campaign pledge, made before he was president. PR #62 does not change it, and the new paper wrapper pairs it with og:description text that says 2.5%. MAJORS: (1) The ledger says judgment inputs were "drafted by a research agent and checked by a second". (5) One of the 12 unverified citations (Verho et al. 2022) is cited for "raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing", but its abstract says "minor employment effects at best" and does not mention wellbeing.

Cost of waiting: revision 1's 9.6% stays live about 12 to 18 more hours (lanes reopen around 05:30 UTC 1 Oct per the brief, not verified, and each job may run up to 6 h). Little else is at stake. What waiting buys: the independent review, the citation check, and the endorsement, passage and trigger research that was meant to set the revision-2 priors. If that research moves the priors, publishing now would force a third headline within days on pages the markets link to.

Lean (the decision is the owner's): fix the blocker and the majors now, since they are copy and asset edits of minutes each. votes.reasoning:
I tried to refute the finding and could not; every part of it reproduced. 1. The live image is the revision-1 card. https://maxghenis.com/ubi-forecast/og-image.png returned HTTP 200 as image/png. Its sha1 is 5448f92c675f2d1cd405c78955b196c3342628a9 and its git blob is 7e5a4754fea510e1f36e836040f8abd1eaf3b13e. I viewed it: it reads "Pay to the order of every adult in the United States / $6,000 a year / 2040", with "9.6%" in the box and "chance, as of September 2026" beneath. 2. The repo copy is the same file. At revision-2 HEAD 2b027ba (the PR #1 head), dashboard/og/og-image.png has the same sha1 and blob. dashboard/og/og.html line 22 hard-codes `
9.6%
`, and nothing regenerates the image: dashboard/build.js has no og step, and the only other script is dashboard/scripts/fetch_markets.py. Revision 2's value in paper/_variables.yml is usa_2040: "2.5%". 3. PR #62 does not replace the image. At PR #62 head 48234513, public/ubi-forecast/og-image.png has blob 7e5a4754..., the same as on master. The PR's file list does not include it; it changes only index.html, paper/index.html, paper/web/index.html, paper/web/index.pdf and vercel.json. 4. Both revision-2 pages point at that image. PR #62's public/ubi-forecast/index.html sets og:image on line 13 and twitter:image on line 18 to that URL, and paper/index.html sets og:image on line 13. The paper wrapper's og:description says "2.5% by 2040 and 7.4% by 2050". The sources match: dashboard/src/template.html (lines 13 and 18) and paper/scripts/build_wrapper.py (line 35). The result is that any shared preview of the revision-2 dashboard or paper would show a US $6,000-by-2040 chance of 9.6%, labeled as current ("as of September 2026"). That is about four times the published 2.5%, and on the paper link it would sit next to a description that says 2.5%. This meets the blocker definition: it would show readers a materially false headline number. The engine's numbers are not wrong, but the card is the most-seen part of a share. The other "9.6%" strings in app.js line 379 and paper/index.qmd line 186 are deliberate references to revision 1, so they do not mitigate this. The fix the finding proposes is sound. (4) README.md:30 says "365 checks". country_research.json has 332 verdict entries on both branches, and the paper (index.qmd:108) and the dashboard (app.js:372) both say 332. This mismatch was already on main.

- 9.6% for the same $6,000-by-2040 event, with no label saying it is revision 1;
- a sensitivity table of inputs that no longer exist;
- a script that crashes;
- a trigger described as "economist-attributed", which is exactly the kind of assumption revision 2 says it removed.

The paper also discloses revision 1's 9.6% (index.qmd revision note), so a reader who reads both can reconcile them. Both PRs are OPEN, MERGEABLE and not drafts, so the fix fits inside the wait.

findings.claim: 'Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]'
findings.evidence: The Crossref abstract for 10.1257/pol.20200143 says that replacing minimum unemployment benefits with a basic income 'has minor employment effects at best' and that 'days in employment remained statistically unchanged in the first year'. It says nothing about wellbeing. This is 1 of the 12 keys in paper/references_PENDING_VERIFICATION.txt, and all 12 are cited in index.qmd at lines 62, 88, 118 and 120. All 12 DOIs match Crossref on title, authors, year, volume and pages. The Parolin & Siöland and Dermont & Weisstanner abstracts support their line-118 claims. The Roosma & van Oorschot range 'about a third to four-fifths' is not in that paper's abstract: not verified. I read abstracts only.

votes.reasoning:
The finding holds, and it holds more firmly than an abstract-only check could show, because I read the full working-paper text.

1. The sentence is in the repo and in the staged publish. paper/index.qmd line 120 on branch revision-2 says "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]". The same sentence is in the paper HTML that maxghenis.com PR #62 stages (public/ubi-forecast/paper/web/index.html at head 48234513).

2. The cited source does not support "improved wellbeing". The Crossref abstract for 10.1257/pol.20200143 covers employment only; the paper's subtitle is "Employment Responses". I also read the full text of VATT Working Paper 142 (March 2021), whose abstract matches the published one word for word. It reports no wellbeing, life-satisfaction or mental-health outcomes. Its only mention of wellbeing ("subjective well-being") describes Haushofer and Shapiro's Kenya study in the literature review.

3. "Raised employment slightly" overstates the authors' own conclusion. They estimate an insignificant +1.5 days in year 1 (95% CI -2.3 to 5.4). Year 2 shows a significant +6.6 days (95% CI 1.3 to 11.9), but the authors say it "cannot be attributed to the basic income experiment alone" because of the 2018 unemployment benefit reform. Their stated main finding is that the experiment "had no detectable employment effect in the first year". The positive point estimates keep this half from being outright false, but it misstates what the source concludes.

4. The wellbeing fact itself seems true, just cited to the wrong source. My web search returned a Finnish ministry release and a VATT release, both headed "small employment effects, better perceived economic security and mental wellbeing". I saw only the search summary and did not open either page. Per that summary, the 2020 final evaluation reported higher life satisfaction and less mental strain. So the fix is to re-cite the claim, not delete it. The same Edward Elgar volume that holds kangas2021feasibility is the likely home for a wellbeing chapter, but I did not verify that.

5. The finding's side claims check out. references_PENDING_VERIFICATION.txt lists 12 keys, including verho2022removing. My grep shows every one of them cited in index.qmd at lines 62, 88, 118 or 120 only. Crossref has the correct title, authors, volume (14), pages (501-522) and year (2022) for Verho et al.

Severity: this is a claim the cited source does not support, in a paper that is about to be published. It does not touch any headline number. That matches "major" in the task's rubric. The underlying fact is likely true, so this is a wrong citation rather than a false statement, which keeps it from being a blocker.

votes.reasoning:
The finding is real, and a reader would see it: the sentence ships in the staged publication. Line 120 of paper/index.qmd reads "Finland's experiment raised employment slightly and improved wellbeing [@verho2022removing]". The same sentence appears word for word in public/ubi-forecast/paper/web/index.html on the ubi-revision-2 branch of maxghenis.com PR #62.

The cited paper does not support either half.

1. **Employment.** The authors' main finding is "no detectable employment effect in the first year". That year's point estimate is 1.5 days (95% CI -2.3 to 5.4) against a control mean of 49 days. The second-year estimate is 6.6 days and statistically significant. The authors say it "cannot be attributed to the basic income experiment alone" because the 2018 unemployment-benefit reform happened at the same time, and they "focus primarily on the first-year result". The abstract's summary is "minor employment effects at best". Saying the experiment "raised employment slightly" presents a confounded second-year estimate as the finding, the opposite of how the authors frame it.
2. **Wellbeing.** The paper does not study it. Its only mention of "well-being" is about GiveDirectly in Kenya (Haushofer and Shapiro).

The project's own research note contradicts the manuscript too. research/citations_raw.json says to use this source "for the finding that the only nationwide randomized BI trial produced minor employment effects at best". The manuscript sentence drifted from that note.

**Impact.**
- No number changes. The paragraph opens "Evidence on effects enters only through feasibility", so no model input depends on it, and the dashboard has no Finland or wellbeing copy (I searched the whole repo).
- It is still a wrong claim tied to a named peer-reviewed source. Any reader who follows the citation or knows the Finnish literature will find the source says close to the opposite. That hurts a paper whose stated goal is that everything be falsifiable.
- The wellbeing result is plausibly true elsewhere, in Kela's evaluation, but the paper cites the wrong source for it.

This meets the rubric's "major": a wrong or unsupported claim that should be fixed before publishing but does not change a headline number. It is not a blocker because it is peripheral context rather than a forecast claim, and the fix is one sentence. Queued citation verification is no reason to leave it. The source is open-access and has now been read, so the fix does not need to wait for the ubi-cite-verify job.
